t: Cloud Computing · L1 · The Era of Cloud Computing
p: CSTE4103 · CLOUD COMPUTING Lecture 1 The Era of Cloud Computing Motivation for the Cloud · The Power Wall · Racks & Data Centers · Elastic Computing · Multi-tenant Clouds · IaaS / PaaS / SaaS / DaaS 4th-Year Cybersecurity Engineering · Week 1 · Semester 7 Dept. of ICT — Polytechnic College for Engineering Specializations, MTU TODAY'S ROADMAP Learning Objectives 1 Explain why computing moved from on-premise servers to the cloud 2 Describe the Power Wall and why it forced a shift to distributed systems 3 Understand elastic computing and multi-tenant architectures 4 Classify cloud services: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, and DaaS 5 Recognize how each service model changes the security responsibility boundary 2 / 14

1. MOTIVATION Before the Cloud: The Bare-Metal Era A Traditional Data Room High CAPEX: hardware purchased up front, before demand is known Capacity is fixed — over-provision (waste) or under-provision (outage) Every patch, backup, and physical control is the owner's job alone One organization → one server rack → fixed capacity Scaling means buying, shipping, and racking new machines — weeks, not minutes Bought, owned, cooled, patched, and physically secured by the organization itself. 3 / 14 2. THE POWER WALL Why We Stopped Making Chips Faster Single-core clock speed (illustrative) The Power Wall Faster clock speeds mean exponentially more heat and power draw. Around the mid-2000s, chipmakers hit a physical ceiling: a single processor could no longer get meaningfully faster without melting itself. The industry's answer: stop chasing raw speed. Add more cores, and more machines, and spread the work across them — parallel and distributed computing. This is the physical reason cloud data centers are built from thousands of ordinary machines rather than one extraordinary one. 1995 2000 2005 2010 2015 2020 Flattens after ~2005 — heat & power limits, not lack of demand 4 / 14

3. SCALING OUT Racks of Server Computers The horizontal answer to the Power Wall: instead of one powerful machine, use many ordinary ones, organized for scale. Server Rack → A single physical machine — CPU, RAM, disk, NIC Aisle / Pod Data Center → 10–40+ servers stacked in one cabinet, sharing power & networking → Rows of racks grouped for airflow, power, and network design Thousands of racks — the physical body of "the cloud" Full data-center design (cooling, North-South/East-West traffic, fat-tree & leaf-spine networks) is covered in Week 3 — today, just the concept. 5 / 14 4. ELASTICITY Elastic Computing Definition The ability to automatically acquire more computing resources when demand rises, and release them when demand falls — paying only for what is actually used. Example — Exam-Result Portal Traffic Servers scale up automatically for the traffic spike, then scale back down — no manual purchase, no idle hardware afterward. Contrast with the bare-metal era: capacity there was fixed at purchase time, months before it was needed. Normal day Result day (auto-scaled) Scaled back 6 / 14

5. SHARED INFRASTRUCTURE Multi-tenant Clouds Definition: many independent customers ("tenants") share the same underlying physical hardware, while each tenant's data and workloads remain logically isolated. One Physical Host Tenant A isolated VM / container Security Angle Tenant B isolated VM / container Tenant C Shared hardware means a new attack surface: hypervisor escapes, side-channel attacks (e.g. cache timing), and noisy-neighbor resource abuse — none of which exist in a single-tenant, bare-metal setup. isolated VM / container Isolation is enforced in software (hypervisor / container runtime) — its correctness is now a core security control. 7 / 14 6. SERVICE MODELS IaaS · PaaS · SaaS · DaaS IaaS PaaS SaaS DaaS Infrastructure as a Service Platform as a Service Software as a Service Desktop as a Service You manage: OS, runtime, apps, data You manage: apps & data only You manage: your data & access You manage: your files & profile Left → Right: the provider takes on more of the management burden — and more of the security responsibility along with it. 8 / 14

IAAS Infrastructure as a Service The provider supplies raw compute, storage, and networking — virtualized hardware. You install and manage everything above it. Application Runtime / Data Examples: Amazon EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine OS Virtualization You choose the OS, install your own stack, configure networking rules Servers Maximum control and flexibility — maximum operational responsibility Storage Networking Typical users: system administrators, DevOps teams, infrastructure engineers Customer-managed Provider-managed 9 / 14 PAAS Platform as a Service The provider manages the OS, runtime, and middleware. You deploy code and data — the platform handles patching, scaling, and availability. Application Runtime / Data Examples: Azure App Service, Google App Engine, Heroku OS Developers push code; the platform builds, deploys, and scales it Virtualization Servers No OS patching, no server maintenance — faster development cycles Storage Typical users: application developers, small engineering teams Networking 10 / 14

SAAS Software as a Service The provider runs the entire application. You simply use it — typically through a browser — and manage only your own data and user access. Application Runtime / Data Examples: Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Zoom OS Virtualization Nothing to install, patch, or scale — the vendor owns the full stack Servers Your responsibility narrows to: account security, access control, data you upload Storage Networking Typical users: everyone — end users, administrators, entire organizations Customer still owns: identity & access management, data classification, and end-user device security. 11 / 14 DAAS Desktop as a Service A complete virtual desktop — OS, applications, and user profile — streamed from the cloud to any device. Examples Where DaaS sits Amazon WorkSpaces, Windows 365, Citrix DaaS Why organizations use it DaaS is really SaaS applied to the desktop itself: the provider manages the full OS + app stack, and the customer manages only data, identity, and what the user does inside the session. Consistent, centrally-managed desktops for remote or contract staff; sensitive data never leaves the data center — the endpoint only displays pixels. This last point matters for security: a lost or compromised laptop does not mean lost data. Typical users: remote workforces, BPO/call centers, students needing access to specialized lab software from any device. 12 / 14

BRINGING IT TOGETHER Why This Matters for a Security Engineer Shared Responsibility Every cloud service has a line: what the provider secures, and what you secure. That line moves with the service model — know exactly where it sits before you design a control around it. New Attack Surface Multi-tenancy, hypervisors, and APIs are attack surfaces that simply did not exist in the bare-metal era. Elasticity Cuts Both Ways Auto-scaling defends against load spikes — but a misconfigured resource can also scale an attacker's cost-abuse or cryptomining attack. 13 / 14 WRAP-UP Summary & Next Week Today, in one sentence: The Power Wall forced computing to scale horizontally, giving rise to elastic, multi-tenant clouds offered at four levels of abstraction — IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, DaaS — each shifting the security boundary. Next Week — Week 2 Types of Clouds and Their Providers: Private vs. Public Cloud, Provider Lock-in, Hybrid Cloud, Multi-Cloud, and Hyperscale providers. Discussion Questions • If a bank moves its core banking app from bare-metal to SaaS, what security controls does it lose direct control over? • Where would you place a national ID database on the IaaS–DaaS spectrum, and why? 14 / 14

t: Cloud Computing · L2 · Types of Clouds, Providers & Data Centers
p: CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing Types of Clouds, Providers, and Data Centers Private, Public, Hybrid, Multi-Cloud, Lock-in, Hyperscale, and Data Center Essentials Lecture 2 • Cybersecurity Engineering — 4th Year Dr. Ruaa Ali Khamees • ICT Department Polytechnic College for Engineering Specializations – Baghdad, Middle Technical University LECTURE 2 • OVERVIEW Learning Objectives 1 Deployment models 2 Define private, public, hybrid, and multi-cloud deployments. 3 Provider lock-in Compare them by ownership, cost, control, and security responsibility. 4 Explain what causes lock-in and how to reduce it. 5 Hyperscale and data centers Describe hyperscale and the building blocks of a data center. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing Private vs public Hybrid vs multi-cloud Distinguish the two and know when each one fits. 6 Security lens Choose a deployment model by weighing risk and compliance. 2

1 — FRAMING Two Questions About Any Cloud Lecture 1 answered the first question. Today we answer the second. Service model Deployment model WHAT do you get from the provider? WHO owns the infrastructure, and WHO shares it? IaaS • PaaS • SaaS • DaaS Private • Public • Hybrid • Multi-cloud (Lecture 1) (Today) Example: Gmail is SaaS (service model) delivered from a public cloud (deployment model). The two choices are independent. 3 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 2 — DEPLOYMENT MODELS Private Cloud Cloud infrastructure dedicated to a single organization, run in its own data center or in a provider's dedicated space. Characteristics Typical technologies • One tenant: no sharing with other customers • OpenStack • Full control of hardware, network, and policy • VMware vSphere • High upfront cost (CapEx) and in-house staff • Proxmox (our Labs 7–8) • Elasticity limited by the hardware you own • Kubernetes on your own servers ⚠ Security angle: You own the whole stack, so you also own the whole security burden: physical access, patching, monitoring, and incident response. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 4

2 — DEPLOYMENT MODELS Public Cloud Infrastructure owned and operated by a provider and rented to many customers (tenants) over the internet. Characteristics Major providers • Multi-tenant: resources shared and isolated logically • Pay-as-you-go (OpEx), no upfront hardware • Near-instant elasticity and global regions • The provider secures the infrastructure layers Amazon Web Services Microsoft Azure Google Cloud Also: Alibaba Cloud, Oracle Cloud, IBM Cloud, DigitalOcean ⚠ Security angle: Shared responsibility: the provider secures the cloud, you secure what you put in it. Misconfiguration is a leading cause of public-cloud breaches. 5 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 2 — DEPLOYMENT MODELS Private vs Public at a Glance Aspect Private cloud Public cloud Ownership Single organization Provider; shared by many tenants Cost model High upfront (CapEx) Pay-as-you-go (OpEx) Elasticity Limited by owned hardware Near-unlimited, on demand Control Full Limited to what the provider exposes Time to deploy Weeks to months Minutes Security duty Entirely the organization Shared with the provider Best for Strict compliance, steady workloads Variable demand, fast growth CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 6

2 — DEPLOYMENT MODELS Hybrid Cloud Private cloud / on-premises Public cloud VPN / dedicated link Sensitive data Burst capacity Legacy systems Web front-ends ⇄ Regulated workloads Analytics and backups Cloud bursting Data residency Gradual migration Run normally in-house; rent public capacity only for peaks. Keep regulated data local; use the public cloud for everything else. Move workloads to the cloud step by step, not all at once. ⚠ Security angle: The link between the two worlds is a new attack surface; encrypt it and keep policies consistent on both sides. 7 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 2 — DEPLOYMENT MODELS Multi-Cloud Using two or more public cloud providers for different workloads, or for the same workload. Your applications AWS Azure Google Cloud Benefits Challenges • Less lock-in • More skills needed • Resilience to one provider's outage • Different IAM and tools • • Best service for each task Egress fees between clouds Hybrid is not the same as multi-cloud Hybrid = private + public, working together. Multi-cloud = two or more public providers. A company can be both at the same time. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 8

3 — PROVIDERS Provider Lock-in Lock-in means switching providers becomes so costly or difficult that you stay even when you would rather leave. What creates it How to reduce it • Proprietary services and APIs (managed databases, serverless) • Containers and Kubernetes for portable workloads • Data gravity: large datasets are slow and costly to move out • Infrastructure as Code (e.g., Terraform) • Egress (data-out) fees • Open standards and portable data formats • Team skills and tooling tied to one platform • Regular exports and tested backups • Long-term contracts and commitments • A written exit plan before you sign ⚠ Security angle: Lock-in is also an availability and resilience risk: if the provider has an outage or changes its terms, you have no quick alternative. 9 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 3 — PROVIDERS Hyperscale Region Availability Zone A What makes it hyperscale Availability Zone B Availability Zone C Data center Data center Data center Data center Data center Data center • Data centers with very large server counts • Global footprint of regions and zones • Custom hardware, chips, and networking • Automation of almost everything Why it matters Economies of scale lower unit prices and allow services no single company could build alone. Zones are separate facilities in one region, linked by fast private networks, so one failure does not take everything down. ⚠ Security angle: Concentration risk: a large share of the internet depends on a few hyperscalers, so one failure can ripple widely. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 10

4 — INSIDE THE DATA CENTER Racks, Aisles, and Pods Rack Hot aisle: warm exhaust air leaves A standard frame (about 42U) holding servers and a top-of-rack switch. Aisle Cold aisle: cool air enters The space between rows, used to control the flow of cool and hot air. Pod Hot aisle: warm exhaust air leaves A group of racks sharing power, cooling, and network uplinks: the unit you add as you grow. Rows face each other so cold air is drawn in from the middle and hot air is collected at the outer aisles. 11 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 4 — INSIDE THE DATA CENTER Power and Cooling Utility grid → UPS Backup generator → PDU → Rack UPS = batteries that bridge the gap until the generator starts. PDU = distributes power to each rack. Cooling • Hot/cold aisle containment keeps air streams apart • Air-conditioning units (CRAC/CRAH) move the heat out • Chilled water and liquid cooling for very dense racks • Site and climate choices can cut cooling cost PUE PUE = total facility power ÷ power used by IT equipment. 1.0 is the ideal; the lower the value, the less energy is wasted on cooling and power losses. ⚠ Security angle: Availability is a security property: redundant power and cooling paths protect against outages and sabotage. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 12

4 — INSIDE THE DATA CENTER North-South vs East-West Traffic North-South Users / Internet Traffic between users outside and servers inside the data center. ↕ North-South East-West Data center Server 1 Server 2 Server 3 Traffic between servers inside: storage replication, microservice calls, data processing. It is usually the larger share in cloud data centers. Server 4 ⚠ Security angle: Perimeter firewalls rarely see east-west traffic, so attackers move laterally. Micro-segmentation and zero trust limit it. East-West: server to server 13 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 4 — INSIDE THE DATA CENTER Fat-Tree and Leaf-Spine Design Why leaf-spine Spine 1 Spine 2 Spine 3 Leaf 1 Leaf 2 Leaf 3 Leaf 4 Servers Servers Servers Servers • Every leaf connects to every spine • Any two servers are the same hops apart: predictable latency • More servers: add leaves. More bandwidth: add spines • Many equal-cost paths, so one failed link barely matters Fat-Tree The idea of many parallel equal paths with full bandwidth. Leaf-spine is a common practical form of it. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 14

4 — INSIDE THE DATA CENTER Unified Network and Security Takeaways Unified data center network Security takeaways One Ethernet-based fabric carries user, storage, and management traffic instead of a separate network for each. • Control physical access to racks and cages • Separate the management network from user and storage traffic • Watch east-west traffic, not only the perimeter • Treat power and cooling redundancy as availability controls • Fewer devices and cables • Simpler operations • Needs priorities and isolation so traffic types do not interfere Next: all this shared hardware is sliced up by virtualization. That is Lecture 3. 15 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 5 — SECURITY LENS Security Across Deployment Models Model Who secures what Key risk Typical controls Private The organization, all layers Under-resourced patching and monitoring Hardening, SIEM, physical access control Public Shared with the provider Misconfigured storage and IAM Least privilege, MFA, encryption, posture checks Hybrid Both sides, plus the link Weak link, inconsistent policies Encrypted tunnels, unified identity, segmentation Multi-cloud Each provider separately Bigger attack surface, tool sprawl Central identity, policy-as-code, unified logging Rule of thumb: the more places your data lives, the more consistent your identity and logging must be. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 16

6 — APPLY IT Choosing a Model: Mini Case The scenario A national bank must keep customer records inside the country. Its mobile app has unpredictable peaks on salary days and holidays, and the board worries about depending on one vendor. Is the data regulated? 1 Points toward private or hybrid. Is demand predictable? 2 Unpredictable favors public elasticity. Which deployment model would you recommend, and why? Do we have staff to run it? 3 No staff makes private harder. Can we depend on one vendor? 4 No points toward multi-cloud. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 17 SUMMARY Summary and Next Week Key points • Private = control and responsibility; public = elasticity and shared responsibility. • Hybrid mixes private and public; multi-cloud mixes several public providers. • Lock-in grows with proprietary services and data gravity; plan your exit early. • Hyperscalers deliver scale and low cost but concentrate risk; racks, pods, power, cooling, and leaf-spine networks make it work. • Pick the model by data sensitivity, demand pattern, skills, and risk. Next week (Lecture 3) Virtual Machines and Containers: approaches to virtualization, hypervisors, VM migration, Docker containers and their components. Reference: Comer, D. E. (2021). The Cloud Computing Book. CRC Press. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 18

t: Cloud Computing · L3 · Virtual Machines & Containers
p: CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing Virtual Machines and Containers Virtualization, Hypervisors, VM Migration, Docker, and Container Security Lecture 3 • Cybersecurity Engineering — 4th Year Dr. Ruaa Ali Khamees • ICT Department Polytechnic College for Engineering Specializations – Baghdad, Middle Technical University LECTURE 3 • OVERVIEW Learning Objectives 1 Why virtualize 2 Explain consolidation, isolation, and elasticity. 3 VM lifecycle Compare Type 1 and Type 2, and full, para, and hardware-assisted virtualization. 4 Describe snapshots, cloning, and live migration. 5 Docker Name its components and trace the build, ship, run workflow. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing Hypervisors Containers Explain namespaces and cgroups, and how containers differ from VMs. 6 Security Compare isolation strength and attack surface of VMs and containers. 2

1 — WHY VIRTUALIZE One Server, Many Machines Last week's racks hold physical servers. Virtualization slices each one into isolated virtual machines, which is what makes cloud sharing possible. Consolidation Isolation Elasticity Typical physical servers idle at low utilization. Packing many VMs on one host raises utilization and cuts hardware, power, and space. Each VM has its own OS and resources. A crash or compromise in one should not reach its neighbors. A VM is software: create, clone, resize, or move it in minutes. This is the engine behind on-demand IaaS. Link to Lab 3: you will see this on your own PC with VMware Workstation. 3 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 2 — HYPERVISORS Type 1 and Type 2 Hypervisors A hypervisor (virtual machine monitor) creates VMs and shares CPU, memory, and I/O among them. Type 1 — bare metal Type 2 — hosted VM 1 | VM 2 | VM 3 VM 1 | VM 2 Hypervisor Hypervisor (an application) Hardware Host OS (Windows / Linux) Hardware Examples: ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, Xen — used in data centers. Examples: VMware Workstation, VirtualBox — used on desktops and labs. Cloud providers run Type 1 (KVM-based or custom). CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 4

2 — HYPERVISORS Approaches to Virtualization Approach How it works Guest OS changed? Trade-off Full virtualization Hypervisor emulates the full hardware; binary translation for privileged instructions. No Compatible, but slower Para-virtualization Guest knows it is virtual and calls the hypervisor directly (hypercalls). Yes Fast, needs modified OS Hardware-assisted CPU extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) trap privileged operations in hardware. No Fast and compatible; today's default ⚠ Check: If Intel VT-x / AMD-V is disabled in BIOS, 64-bit guests may fail to start in your lab. Enable it first. 5 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 2 — HYPERVISORS What the Hypervisor Virtualizes CPU Memory I/O Schedules vCPUs onto physical cores. Over-subscription lets total vCPUs exceed cores, which is efficient but can cause contention. Maps guest memory to host memory. Techniques such as ballooning and page sharing reclaim unused RAM. Presents virtual disks and virtual NICs. Disks are often files on shared storage; NICs connect to virtual switches. Security consequence: whoever controls the hypervisor controls every VM above it. It is the most valuable target on the host, so keep it minimal and patched. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 6

3 — VIRTUAL MACHINES VM Lifecycle: Snapshots and Clones A VM is mostly files: virtual disks plus a configuration. That is why VMs are easy to copy and recover. Create Run Snapshot Clone Retire Pick vCPU, RAM, disk, network; install or use an image. Start, pause, suspend, resize resources. Save the state at a point in time to roll back after a mistake or failed update. Copy a VM or a golden template to deploy many identical machines. Delete the VM and securely wipe its disks. ⚠ Security: Snapshots and clones keep old data and old secrets (keys, passwords, unpatched software). Treat them like backups and protect them the same way. 7 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 3 — VIRTUAL MACHINES VM Migration Moving a VM between hosts lets the provider balance load, patch hosts, and evacuate failing hardware. Cold migration Live migration Shut the VM down, copy it, start it on the new host. Simple, but there is downtime. Move a running VM with almost no downtime; users usually do not notice. Live migration, pre-copy method 1. Copy all memory pages while the VM keeps running 2. Re-copy pages that changed (repeat) 3. Pause briefly, send the last pages and CPU state 4. Resume on the new host Memory is sent over the network: encrypt the migration channel. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 8

4 — CONTAINERS Containers: Isolation Without a Guest OS A container is an ordinary process on the host kernel, wrapped by two Linux features that limit what it can see and use. Namespaces — what it can SEE cgroups — what it can USE Separate views of processes (PID), network, mounts, hostname, and users. Inside, the container thinks it is alone. Limits CPU, memory, and I/O per container so one cannot starve the others. Because there is no guest OS, a container starts in seconds, uses megabytes, and you can pack many more per host than VMs. The price is a shared kernel. 9 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 4 — CONTAINERS VM Stack vs Container Stack Virtual machines Containers App A | App B | App C App A | App B | App C Guest OS | Guest OS | Guest OS Container engine (Docker) Hypervisor Host OS kernel (shared) Host hardware Host hardware Each VM carries a full OS (GBs, minutes to boot). Containers share one kernel (MBs, seconds to start). CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 10

4 — CONTAINERS VMs vs Containers Aspect Virtual machine Container Isolation Strong: separate kernel per VM Weaker: shared host kernel Startup Minutes Seconds Size Gigabytes Megabytes Density per host Tens Hundreds Guest OS Any (Windows, Linux...) Same kernel family as host Best for Legacy apps, strong tenant separation Microservices, CI/CD, scale-out In practice they combine: containers usually run inside VMs in the cloud. 11 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 5 — DOCKER Docker Components Docker packages an application and everything it needs, so it runs the same on a laptop, a lab server, or a cloud VM. Dockerfile Image Container A text recipe: base image, files, commands. Read-only layered template built from the Dockerfile. A running instance of an image, with a thin writable layer. Engine (daemon) Registry Volume / Network Builds images and runs containers on the host. Stores and distributes images (Docker Hub, private registry). Persistent data outside the container; virtual networks between containers. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 12

5 — DOCKER Build, Ship, Run Dockerfile Image docker build → Registry docker push → Container docker pull → # Dockerfile FROM nginx:alpine COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/ # build and run docker build -t mysite . docker run -d -p 8080:80 mysite What happened: the image holds the web server and your page; the container runs it and maps host port 8080 to container port 80. 13 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 6 — SECURITY LENS Isolation and Attack Surface Virtual machines Containers Risks: VM escape through a hypervisor flaw, side-channel attacks between co-located VMs, stale snapshots, VM sprawl. Risks: kernel exploit reaches every container, privileged containers, vulnerable or untrusted images, secrets baked into images. Good practices • Patch the hypervisor and host kernel; keep them minimal. • Use trusted, scanned images; pin versions; never store secrets in an image. • Do not run containers as root or with --privileged; drop capabilities. • Separate sensitive workloads on different hosts or inside VMs. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 14

7 — APPLY IT VM or Container? Mini Case The scenario A university hosts three things: (1) an old Windows-only grading system, (2) a student web portal with traffic spikes at registration, (3) a lab where outside researchers run untrusted code. Needs another OS or old kernel? 1 Points to a VM. Needs fast scale-out? 2 Points to containers. Choose VM or container for each, and justify it. Runs untrusted code? 3 Strong isolation: a VM. Can we combine? 4 Containers inside VMs is common. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 15 SUMMARY Summary and Next Week Key points • Virtualization enables consolidation, isolation, and elasticity. • Type 1 hypervisors run on hardware; Type 2 run on a host OS. Hardware-assist is the norm. • VMs are files: snapshot, clone, and live-migrate them, and protect those copies. • Containers share the host kernel via namespaces and cgroups: light and fast, weaker isolation. • Docker: Dockerfile builds an image, a registry stores it, an engine runs it as a container. Next week (Lecture 4) Virtual Networks and Virtual Storage: virtual switches, overlays and VLANs, SDN, block, file, and object storage. Reference: Comer, D. E. (2021). The Cloud Computing Book. CRC Press. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 16

t: Cloud Computing · L4 · Virtual Networks & Virtual Storage
p: CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing Virtual Networks and Virtual Storage Virtual Switches, VLAN and VXLAN, Overlays, SDN and OpenFlow, and Block, File, and Object Storage Lecture 4 • Cybersecurity Engineering — 4th Year Dr. Ruaa Ali Khamees • ICT Department Polytechnic College for Engineering Specializations – Baghdad, Middle Technical University LECTURE 4 • OVERVIEW Learning Objectives 1 Virtual networking 2 Explain how VMs connect through virtual NICs and virtual switches, and the main network modes. 3 Underlay and overlay Compare them, and explain why clouds need more than VLANs. 4 Describe how tunnels build virtual networks on top of a physical IP network. 5 Storage types Compare block, file, and object storage, and traditional versus software-defined storage. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing VLAN and VXLAN SDN and OpenFlow Describe the control plane and data plane split, and how flow tables work. 6 Security Evaluate segmentation, encryption, and access risks in virtual networks and storage. 2

1 — WHY From Cables to Software Lecture 3 gave us thousands of VMs on a few hosts. Nobody can re-cable a data center each time a VM appears, so the network must be built in software too. Isolation per tenant Agility Mobility Each customer needs a private network that other customers cannot see, even on the same physical switches. A virtual network, subnet, or firewall rule is created in seconds by an API call, not by a technician with a cable. When a VM live-migrates, it keeps its IP address and network policy. The network must follow the VM. Link to Lab 3: the NAT network that gave your Ubuntu VM internet access was a virtual network created by VMware in software. 3 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 2 — VIRTUAL NETWORKS Virtual NICs and Virtual Switches Physical host How it works VM 1 VM 2 VM 3 vNIC vNIC vNIC • Each VM gets one or more virtual NICs with their own MAC address • The vSwitch forwards frames between VMs on the same host in software • Frames for other hosts leave through the physical uplink Virtual switch (vSwitch) Examples: VMware vSwitch, Hyper-V vSwitch, Linux bridge, Open vSwitch (OVS), Docker bridge. Physical NIC (uplink) Physical switch and the data center network CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing ⚠ Security angle: Traffic between two VMs on one vSwitch never meets the physical firewall. Use port security and limit promiscuous mode. 4

2 — VIRTUAL NETWORKS Network Modes: What You Choose in Lab 3 Mode How the VM connects Reaches the internet Reachable from the LAN Typical use Bridged Acts like a separate device on your real network with its own LAN address Yes Yes Servers other machines must reach NAT (used in Lab 3) Shares the host's address; VMware translates addresses Yes No (unless port forwarding) Labs, safe default for learning Host-only Private network between the VM and the host only No No Isolated testing, malware analysis ⚠ Security angle: Choose the least exposed mode that works. Bridged puts the VM directly on your LAN. Docker's default bridge network also uses NAT for outbound traffic. 5 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 3 — SEGMENTATION AND OVERLAYS VLAN: One Switch, Many Networks How it works PC PC PC PC PC PC One physical switch VLAN 10 Students VLAN 20 Staff • Access ports belong to one VLAN • Trunk ports carry several VLANs, each frame tagged with 802.1Q (4 bytes) • The VLAN ID has 12 bits: 1 to 4094 usable • Different VLANs talk only through a router or Layer 3 switch VLAN 30 Servers Same cables and switch, three separate broadcast domains. Why VLANs are not enough for the cloud: only 4094 IDs, and each VLAN is a flat Layer 2 domain tied to one switched network. A cloud with thousands of tenants needs a different tool. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 6

3 — SEGMENTATION AND OVERLAYS Underlay and Overlay OVERLAY: the tenant sees one simple virtual network Host 1 Host 2 UNDERLAY routed IP network (leaf-spine) VM A 10.0.0.5 VM B 10.0.0.9 1 Send 2 Wrap 3 Route 4 Unwrap VM A sends a normal frame to VM B. The tunnel endpoint on Host 1 puts it inside an outer packet addressed to Host 2. The underlay routes the outer packet like any IP traffic. Host 2 removes the outer header and delivers the frame to VM B. Like a letter in an envelope: the postal network reads only the outer address. Two tenants can even reuse the same 10.0.0.0/24 range without conflict. 7 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 3 — SEGMENTATION AND OVERLAYS Wrap and Unwrap: The Four Steps Step Where What happens What is on the wire 1 Send VM A, on Host 1 VM A sends a normal frame to VM B. It does not know a tunnel exists. MAC A → MAC B 10.0.0.5 → 10.0.0.9 2 Wrap VTEP on Host 1 Looks up (VNI 5001, MAC B) and finds Host 2. Adds outer Ethernet, IP, UDP 4789, and VXLAN headers (about 50 bytes). 192.168.1.11 → 192.168.1.12 UDP 4789, VNI 5001 + inner frame 3 Route Underlay (leaf-spine) Routes by the outer IP only, like any IP traffic. The UDP source port varies, so flows spread across the spines. Switches see only host to host. Tenant addresses stay hidden. 4 Unwrap VTEP on Host 2 UDP 4789 goes to the VTEP. It reads VNI 5001, removes the outer headers, and delivers by MAC B. The original frame reaches VM B unchanged. The reply from VM B takes the same path in reverse: Host 2 wraps, the underlay routes, Host 1 unwraps. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 8

3 — SEGMENTATION AND OVERLAYS VXLAN: Layer 2 over Layer 3 VXLAN wraps the tenant's whole Ethernet frame inside a UDP packet, so a virtual Layer 2 network can span any routed IP fabric. Added by the tunnel endpoint (VTEP): about 50 bytes of overhead Outer Ethernet 14 B Outer IP 20 B UDP 8 B, port 4789 VXLAN header 8 B, carries the VNI Inner Ethernet frame the tenant's original frame VNI: 24 bits VTEP MTU pitfall About 16 million virtual networks (2^24), against 4094 for VLAN. VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint. It sits in the host's vSwitch or in a leaf switch and wraps and unwraps frames. The 50 extra bytes can push packets over 1500. Raise the underlay MTU (for example 9000) or lower the VM MTU to about 1450. ⚠ Security angle: VXLAN does not encrypt or authenticate. The VNI separates tenants logically only, so protect the underlay and use IPsec or WireGuard for sensitive traffic. 9 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 3 — SEGMENTATION AND OVERLAYS VLAN vs VXLAN Aspect VLAN VXLAN Segment ID 12 bits: 4094 usable 24-bit VNI: about 16 million How it isolates A tag on the Ethernet frame (802.1Q) The frame is wrapped inside UDP/IP (tunnel) Reach Within one switched Layer 2 network Across a routed IP network, even between sites Overhead 4 bytes About 50 bytes Configuration Switch ports and trunks, often manual Tunnel endpoints plus a control plane (for example BGP EVPN), automated Best for Campus networks, small or fixed data centers Multi-tenant clouds and large data centers In practice they combine: VLANs inside a rack or campus, VXLAN across the data center fabric. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 10

3 — SEGMENTATION AND OVERLAYS Virtual Networks in the Public Cloud Building block What it does AWS Azure Virtual network Your private address space in the cloud VPC VNet Subnet A slice of the network, public or private Subnet Subnet Route table Decides where traffic goes next Route table Route table (UDR) Internet access Inbound and outbound paths to the internet Internet gateway, NAT gateway Public IP, NAT Gateway Firewall rules Allow or deny traffic by port, protocol, and source Security group (stateful), NACL (stateless) NSG (Network Security Group) ⚠ Security angle: Default deny: open only what is needed. Never allow SSH (22) or RDP (3389) from 0.0.0.0/0. Keep databases in private subnets. 11 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 4 — SDN Software-Defined Networking (SDN) Applications routing, firewall, load balancing, monitoring Northbound API (REST) Traditional network Every switch runs its own control logic and is configured one by one. Hard to change, hard to automate. SDN controller = control plane global view, decides the rules Southbound API (OpenFlow) Switches = data plane only forward packets by the rules SDN Logic is centralized in software. One policy change reaches every switch in seconds, through an API. ⚠ Security angle: The controller is a high-value target: whoever controls it controls the whole network. Isolate it, authenticate switches, encrypt the control channel (TLS), and restrict API access. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 12

4 — SDN OpenFlow: Match, Then Act An OpenFlow switch keeps flow tables. Each entry says: if a packet matches these fields, perform this action. Priority Match Action 300 src IP 10.0.1.5, TCP port 22 Drop 200 dst IP 10.0.2.0/24 Forward to port 3 100 VLAN 20 Forward to port 5 0 anything else (table-miss) Send to controller When there is no match • Switch sends a packet-in message to the controller • Controller decides and replies with a flow-mod • Later packets of the flow match the new entry and are forwarded at full speed In practice: Open vSwitch (OVS) is the most common OpenFlow software switch and is used inside many clouds. P4 goes further and lets you program how the switch itself parses packets. 13 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 5 — VIRTUAL STORAGE Block, File, and Object Storage Block File Object Data unit Fixed-size blocks Files in folders Object + metadata + ID Access Raw disk: iSCSI, Fibre Channel NFS, SMB over the network HTTP REST API Examples AWS EBS, Azure Disk, SAN AWS EFS, Azure Files, NAS AWS S3, Azure Blob, MinIO Strength Low latency, high speed Familiar, shared by many users Huge scale, cheap, durable Limit One VM at a time, no sharing Scaling and locking get harder Not for databases or editing in place Best for VM disks, databases Shared folders, home directories Backups, media, logs, big data CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 14

5 — VIRTUAL STORAGE Traditional vs Software-Defined Storage Traditional Software-defined • DAS: disks inside one server • Software runs on commodity servers • NAS: file server on the network • Scale-out: add nodes, capacity and speed grow • SAN: dedicated storage network for block access • Pools many disks into one logical store • Scale-up: buy a bigger, costlier array • Policies by API: replication, snapshots • Vendor hardware and management tools • Examples: Ceph, HDFS, VMware vSAN, MinIO Node 1 Node 2 Node 3 One logical storage pool Replication Erasure coding 3 full copies on different nodes. Simple and fast, but 3x the space. Data split into 4 pieces plus 2 parity: survives 2 failures at 1.5x space. Replication protects against failure, not against deletion or ransomware: keep separate backups. 15 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 6 — SECURITY LENS Security Lens: Networks and Storage Area Typical risk Good practice VLAN and vSwitch VLAN hopping through trunk misconfiguration; east-west traffic that no firewall sees Disable unused ports, fix native VLAN, micro-segmentation Overlay (VXLAN) Unencrypted tunnels; an attacker on the underlay can read or inject traffic Secure the underlay, encrypt with IPsec or WireGuard Cloud network rules Security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0; databases exposed to the internet Least privilege, private subnets, regular rule audits SDN controller Single point of control and failure; rogue switches Isolate, TLS, authenticate, redundant controllers Storage Public buckets, unencrypted data, leaked snapshots and backups Block public access, encrypt at rest and in transit, manage keys, versioning CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 16

7 — APPLY IT Mini Case: A University Private Cloud Scenario: a university runs a private cloud for three tenants: Teaching, Research, and Administration. Exam PDFs for 2,000 students, lab VM disks, and a shared Linux home folder must all be stored. Student VMs must never reach the administration network. Q1 Storage type Q2 Segmentation Q3 VLAN or VXLAN Q4 Threats Which type (block, file, object) for each of the three storage needs, and why? How do you keep student VMs away from the administration network? Would VLANs be enough here? When would you move to VXLAN? Name two threats to this design and one control for each. 17 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing SUMMARY Key Takeaways • A virtual switch connects VMs in software; the mode (Bridged, NAT, Host-only) sets exposure • VLANs give 4094 segments at Layer 2; VXLAN gives about 16 million over routed IP • Overlays ride on an underlay; they isolate logically but do not encrypt • SDN separates control from data plane; the controller is a prime target • Block, file, and object storage serve different needs; software-defined storage scales out Next lecture Distributed Systems and Cloud-Native Software: consensus and Raft, consistency and CAP, cloud-native vs conventional, MapReduce, Hadoop, HDFS Midterm exam: 10 November, covering Lectures 1 to 4. Reference: Comer, D. E. (2021). The Cloud Computing Book. CRC Press. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 18

t: Cloud Computing · L5 · Distributed Systems & Cloud-Native
p: CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing Distributed Systems and Cloud-Native Software Consensus and Raft, Consistency and the CAP Theorem, Cloud-Native vs Conventional Software, MapReduce, Hadoop, and HDFS Lecture 5 • Cybersecurity Engineering — 4th Year Dr. Ruaa Ali Khamees • ICT Department Polytechnic College for Engineering Specializations – Baghdad, Middle Technical University LECTURE 5 • OVERVIEW Learning Objectives 1 Why agreement is hard 2 Explain failures in distributed systems and why nodes must reach consensus. 3 Consistency and CAP Describe quorums, Raft leader election, and log replication. 4 Compare consistency levels and apply the CAP theorem to real systems. 5 MapReduce, Hadoop, HDFS Explain the MapReduce model with its math, and the HDFS architecture. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing Raft and Paxos Cloud-native software Contrast cloud-native and conventional software. 6 Security Evaluate security risks of consensus clusters, stale reads, and big data platforms. 2

1 — WHY Why Distribute? One computer cannot hold all the data, serve all the users, or survive its own failure. Clouds spread work across many machines, and that creates new problems. Scale Availability Locality Data and traffic exceed what one server can store or process. Add machines instead of buying a bigger one. If one machine dies, another continues. Replicas keep the service running. Place data near users and near the computation to cut latency. The price: machines fail independently, messages are delayed or lost, and clocks disagree. So how do many machines agree on one answer? That is the topic of today. 3 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 1 — WHY What Can Go Wrong Failure Meaning Example Crash A node stops and may later restart Power loss, kernel panic Message loss or delay A message arrives late, twice, or never Congested link, packet drop Network partition The cluster splits into groups that cannot talk A switch or inter-site link fails Clock skew Nodes disagree about time, so event order is unclear Drifting server clocks Byzantine A node lies or behaves arbitrarily Compromised or buggy node ⚠ Security angle: Raft and Paxos tolerate crashes and lost messages, but not Byzantine nodes. A compromised member can break the guarantees, so membership must be authenticated. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 4

2 — CONSENSUS The Need for Agreement Consensus means a group of nodes agrees on a single value, even when some nodes fail. Many cloud services depend on it. Where it is needed Required properties • Electing one leader (who is in charge?) • Agreement: no two nodes decide differently • A replicated log of operations in the same order • Validity: the decided value was proposed by someone • Distributed locks and configuration • Termination: every working node eventually decides • Committing a transaction across nodes Example: three replicas of a grades database. A client writes grade 85, and another writes 90 at the same moment. All replicas must apply the writes in the same order, or they will end with different data. A known result (FLP) says no algorithm can guarantee agreement in a fully asynchronous network with even one crash. Real protocols use timeouts to work around it. 5 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 2 — CONSENSUS Quorum: The Power of a Majority A cluster of 5 nodes: 3 form a majority N1 N2 Majority (3 of 5): can decide N3 N4 Nodes (N) Majority Failures tolerated 3 2 1 4 3 1 5 3 2 7 4 3 N5 Minority (2 of 5): cannot decide Why it works • Any two majorities share at least one node, so two groups can never decide differently • With N = 2f + 1 nodes, the cluster survives f crashes • A partition leaves at most one side with a majority CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing Use an odd number of nodes. 4 nodes tolerate only 1 failure, the same as 3, and cost more. Spread nodes across failure domains (racks, sites). 6

2 — CONSENSUS Paxos in Brief Paxos (Lamport) is the classic consensus algorithm. It is proven correct but famously hard to understand and implement. Proposer Acceptor Learner Suggests a value and drives the protocol. Votes. A value is chosen when a majority of acceptors accept it. Finds out which value was chosen and applies it. Phase 1: Prepare Phase 2: Accept Proposer sends Prepare(n) with a number n. Acceptors reply Promise(n): they will ignore lower numbers and report any value already accepted. With a majority of promises, the proposer sends Accept(n, v). Acceptors accept unless they promised a higher number. A majority of accepts means v is chosen. In practice: Multi-Paxos runs many rounds with a stable leader. Used inside Google Chubby and Spanner, and in Ceph monitors. Raft was designed to be easier to understand. 7 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 2 — CONSENSUS Raft: Consensus Made Understandable Raft keeps one strong leader. Clients talk to the leader, and the leader replicates every change to the followers. election timeout Follower majority of votes Candidate Term Leader A logical clock. Each election starts a new term. Two RPCs sees a higher term: steps down RequestVote and AppendEntries. Each node is in exactly one state at a time. A split vote means a new election. Heartbeat Raft splits the problem into three parts: leader election, log replication, and safety. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing An empty AppendEntries the leader sends regularly to stay in charge. 8

2 — CONSENSUS Raft: Leader Election RequestVote (term 4) S1 S2 S3 S4 S5 Follower Follower Candidate Follower Follower 1 Timeout 2 Candidate 3 Vote 4 Leader The leader goes silent. Followers wait a random timeout (about 150 to 300 ms). The first to time out increments the term, votes for itself, and asks others for votes. Each node votes at most once per term, for the first valid request. With 3 of 5 votes, S3 becomes leader and sends heartbeats immediately. Split vote: if two candidates tie, nobody wins. Random timeouts make a second tie unlikely, so a new election resolves it quickly. 9 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 2 — CONSENSUS Raft: Log Replication Leader Follower 1 Follower 2 1: x=1 1: x=1 1: x=1 2: y=2 2: y=2 2: y=2 3: x=3 3: x=3 4: z=5 4: z=5 3: x=3 Why this is safe • Only the leader appends entries, so the order is decided in one place • An entry is committed only after a majority stores it • Followers reject entries that do not match their previous entry, so logs stay consistent • A lagging follower is caught up automatically Entry 4 is on the Leader and Follower 1 = 2 of 3 nodes = majority, so it is committed. 1 Client 2 Append 3 Replicate 4 Commit 5 Reply sends a command to the leader leader adds it to its own log AppendEntries to followers majority stored it: commit apply to state machine, answer client CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 10

2 — CONSENSUS Raft Under Failure Scenario What happens Why it is safe Leader crashes Followers stop receiving heartbeats, time out, and elect a new leader in a higher term Committed entries are on a majority, and the new leader must have them Follower crashes The leader keeps working while a majority is alive. The follower catches up when it returns No decision needs every node Partition 3 | 2 The side with 3 nodes keeps a leader and accepts writes. The side with 2 cannot commit anything Only one side has a majority, so there is no split brain Old leader returns It sees a higher term and steps down to follower Terms order leaders. Stale leaders cannot commit Election restriction: a candidate whose log is behind cannot win. This protects committed data. 11 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 2 — CONSENSUS Where Consensus Lives in the Cloud System Protocol What it keeps in agreement etcd Raft All Kubernetes cluster state, including Secrets Consul Raft Service discovery and configuration ZooKeeper ZAB (Paxos-like) Coordination for Hadoop, Kafka, HBase: locks, leaders Ceph Paxos The cluster map held by the monitors Spanner, CockroachDB Paxos, Raft Replicated data ranges in a global SQL database Link to Lecture 4: SDN controller clusters and storage metadata also rely on consensus. Rule of thumb: use a proven system such as etcd, do not write your own consensus. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 12

3 — CONSISTENCY AND CAP Consistency Levels Level Guarantee Example Cost Strong (linearizable) Every read returns the latest write, as if there were one copy Bank balance, leader lock Highest latency; may refuse requests during a partition Sequential Everyone sees operations in the same order, not necessarily in real time Replicated log Slightly cheaper than strong Causal If A caused B, everyone sees A before B A comment appears after its post Moderate Eventual Replicas converge if writes stop, but reads may be stale meanwhile DNS, like counters, shopping cart Fastest and most available ⚠ Security angle: With eventual consistency, a revoked permission or disabled account can still be honored by a lagging replica. Use strong reads for authorization. 13 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 3 — CONSISTENCY AND CAP The CAP Theorem C Consistency every read sees the latest write What it really says Partitions will happen in any real network. When one does, you must choose: stay consistent (reject some requests) or stay available (answer, maybe with stale data). A Availability every request gets an answer CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing Choice Behavior during a partition Examples CP Minority side refuses requests etcd, ZooKeeper, HBase AP Every side answers, replicas reconcile later Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB P Partition tolerance works despite network splits Without a partition, the trade-off is latency versus consistency (PACELC). 14

4 — CLOUD-NATIVE SOFTWARE Cloud-Native vs Conventional Software Aspect Conventional Cloud-native Architecture One large monolithic application Small independent microservices Runtime Installed on a specific server or VM Containers managed by an orchestrator such as Kubernetes Scaling Scale up: a bigger server Scale out: more small instances, often automatic Failure Avoided; assumes reliable hardware Expected; designed to self-heal State Stored on the local server Services are stateless; state lives in external stores Releases Rare, large, manual Frequent, small, automated (CI/CD) Cloud-native does not mean running in the cloud. It means designed to exploit the cloud: elastic, resilient, automated. 15 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 5 — PARALLEL PROCESSING MapReduce: Divide, Process, Combine When data is too large for one machine, split it, process the pieces in parallel on many machines, then combine the results. MapReduce is a programming model that does this for you. Input Map Block 1 map 1 Shuffle and sort Reduce Output reduce 1 Block 2 map 2 group by key result files reduce 2 Block 3 map 3 Bring computation to the data Failures are handled Map tasks run on the machines that already store the block, so little data crosses the network. If a task fails or is slow, the framework simply runs it again on another machine. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 16

5 — PARALLEL PROCESSING Word Count and the Math of MapReduce Step Data Input lines L1: cloud is big L2: cloud is shared L3: big data is big The model map: (k1, v1) → list(k2, v2) reduce: (k2, list(v2)) → list(v3) Map emits (word, 1) (cloud,1) (is,1) (big,1) (cloud,1) (is,1) (shared,1) (big,1) (data,1) (is,1) (big,1) Shuffle groups by key big:[1,1,1] cloud:[1,1] data:[1] is:[1,1,1] shared:[1] Speedup (Amdahl) S(N) = 1 / ((1 − p) + p / N) p = parallel fraction, N = machines Reduce sums Example: p = 0.95, N = 100 gives S ≈ 16.8, not 100 big 3 cloud 2 data 1 is 3 shared 1 Job time ≈ T_map / N + T_shuffle + T_reduce / R Adding machines shrinks the map and reduce parts, but the shuffle (network) and the serial part do not shrink. That limits speedup. Check: big 3 = 1 (L1) + 2 (L3). Total words 10 = 3 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 1. 17 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 5 — PARALLEL PROCESSING Hadoop and HDFS NameNode: metadata file → blocks → DataNodes DataNode 1 B1 B2 DataNode 2 B1 B3 DataNode 3 B2 B3 Hadoop = three layers • HDFS: distributed storage • YARN: resource scheduling for the cluster • MapReduce: the processing engine DataNode 4 B1 B2 B3 Languages A file is cut into 128 MB blocks. Each block is stored on 3 different DataNodes (replication, as in Lecture 4). Clients read data directly from DataNodes. Java natively. Hadoop Streaming lets any language that reads stdin and writes stdout (Python, Perl) act as mapper or reducer. Hive and Pig add SQL-like and scripting layers. The NameNode is a single point of failure. High availability uses an active and a standby NameNode, with edits kept in a quorum of JournalNodes and failover coordinated by ZooKeeper. That is consensus again. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 18

6 — SECURITY LENS Security Lens: Distributed Systems Area Typical risk Good practice Consensus cluster (etcd, ZooKeeper) Unauthenticated members or clients; whoever controls a majority controls the state, including Kubernetes Secrets Mutual TLS, client authentication, encryption at rest, network isolation Consistency and CAP Stale reads honor revoked permissions; split brain after a bad failover Strong reads for authorization, short token lifetimes, fencing tokens Hadoop and HDFS Open web UIs and RPC ports, default weak authentication, data exposed to every job Kerberos, ACLs, encryption zones, audit logs, isolated network Cloud-native apps Vulnerable images, secrets in code, over-privileged service accounts, supply-chain attacks Image scanning and signing, secret managers, least-privilege accounts MapReduce jobs Untrusted code runs on the cluster; poisoned input data skews results Tenant isolation, quotas, input validation, sandboxing 19 CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 7 — APPLY IT Mini Case: A Results Service Across Three Sites Scenario: a university runs an exam-results service replicated across three sites. It stores grades and a "last login" time for each student. Each night it must analyze 500 GB of access logs to find students with many failed logins. Q1 CP or AP Q2 Raft Q3 MapReduce Q4 Threats Which consistency would you choose for grades, and which for last login? Why? How many Raft nodes, and where? What happens if one site is cut off? Describe the map and reduce functions to count failed logins per student. Name two threats to this design and one control for each. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 20

SUMMARY Key Takeaways • Consensus lets failing nodes agree. A majority quorum makes decisions safe: N = 2f + 1 survives f failures • Raft elects one leader, replicates a log, and commits once a majority stores each entry • CAP: during a partition choose consistency or availability. Pick the level per data type • Cloud-native software is built from small stateless services that expect failure and scale out • MapReduce splits work into map and reduce; HDFS stores replicated blocks; secure both Next lecture Microservices: monoliths in data centers, the microservices approach (pros and cons), granularity, communication protocols, service mesh proxy, and technologies. Reference: Comer, D. E. (2021). The Cloud Computing Book. CRC Press. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 21

t: Cloud Computing · Lab 2 · Hosting Specs & Pricing
p: CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing Lab Lab 2: Hosting Specs and Pricing Read a server specification, then estimate the real monthly cost on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud Week 2 • Cybersecurity Engineering — 4th Year Dr. Ruaa Ali Khamees • ICT Department Polytechnic College for Engineering Specializations – Baghdad, Middle Technical University

LAB 2 • OVERVIEW Objectives and Deliverable By the end you can Your deliverable • Read a hosting specification: vCPU, memory, storage, network, region • One comparison table (monthly and yearly cost) for the same workload on 3 providers • Match a workload to an instance family • A short recommendation: 5 lines, with a security justification • Use the official pricing calculators of three providers • Note the date you took the prices, because they change • Spot hidden costs that raise the final bill • Judge an offer on security and compliance, not price alone CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 2

1 — READING A SPEC Anatomy of a Hosting Specification vCPU Memory (RAM) Storage Virtual processor cores. More cores help parallel work; one busy core limits single-threaded apps. Working memory. Databases and caches are hungry for it; running out causes slowdowns. SSD or HDD, size, and IOPS (operations per second). Fast disks cost more. Network Region and zone OS and licensing Bandwidth and, importantly, outbound data transfer, which is usually billed. Where the server physically lives: affects latency, price, and legal data residency. Linux is usually cheaper; Windows or SQL Server licenses add to the hourly price. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 3

1 — READING A SPEC Instance Families: Match the Workload Family Good for AWS Azure Google Cloud General purpose Web servers, small databases, dev and test M, T D, B E2, N2 Compute optimized Batch processing, encoding, gaming servers C F C2 Memory optimized In-memory caches, large databases, analytics R E M2 Storage optimized High-IOPS databases, data warehouses I, D L Z3 GPU / accelerated Machine learning, rendering P, G N A2, G2 Burstable instances (such as AWS T or Azure B) are cheap but throttle under sustained load; dedicated cores cost more but stay predictable. Series letters are examples; names evolve. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 4

2 — THE TASK Scenario: A University Student Portal A department needs to host a small student portal (web app plus database). Price the same requirement on all three providers. 2 4 GB 50 GB 500 GB Linux 730 h vCPU Memory SSD storage Outbound / month OS Running 24/7 Rules • Pick one region close to Iraq's users, and use the same region logic on all three providers • Choose the cheapest instance that still meets the requirement (not the biggest) • Use on-demand pricing for the main table; note any discount for a 1-year commitment CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 5

3 — DO IT LIVE Using the Official Pricing Calculators AWS Azure Google Cloud Service: EC2 instance Service: Virtual Machines Service: Compute Engine calculator.aws azure.microsoft.com/pricing/calculator cloud.google.com/products/calculator 1 Open the calculator and add the compute service 2 Select the region 3 Choose the instance that matches 2 vCPU / 4 GB 4 Add 50 GB SSD storage 5 Add 500 GB outbound data transfer 6 Record the monthly total and the date CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 6

3 — DO IT LIVE Hidden Costs That Change the Bill The instance price is only the start. Check each of these before you trust a quote. Data egress Public IP addresses Snapshots and backups Load balancer Traffic leaving the cloud is billed; ingress is usually free. Some providers charge for static or in-use public IPs. Every backup consumes billed storage. Billed per hour plus per data processed. Monitoring and logs Support plans Licenses Idle resources Log ingestion and retention add up quickly. Business-grade support is often a percentage of spend. Windows and database licenses raise hourly prices. A forgotten VM or disk keeps billing until deleted. CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing 7

4 — YOUR RESULTS Comparison Table to Fill In Item AWS Azure Google Cloud Region chosen Instance name vCPU / RAM Compute per month Storage per month Data transfer per month Total per month Total per year (×12) 1-year commitment discount Date prices were taken: ____ / ____ / ______ CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing Prices change often, so always cite the date. 8

5 — DECIDE Cheapest Is Not Always Best Before you write your recommendation, check each offer against these security and compliance questions. Region and residency Encryption Identity and access Where will the data physically sit, and is that allowed? Is data encrypted at rest and in transit by default? MFA, roles, and least privilege available out of the box? Availability (SLA) Certifications Backup and exit What uptime percentage is promised, and what is the remedy? ISO 27001, SOC 2, or similar audits published? How easy and how costly is it to back up and leave? Submit: the filled table + a 5-line recommendation that names at least two security reasons. p: CSTE4103 — Cloud Computing • Lab 3 Tutorial 1 Part 1 of 6 Download and Verify the Ubuntu Server ISO Check your PC, download the installer image, and prove it was not corrupted Dr. Ruaa Ali Khamees • Middle Technical University

PART 1 OF 6 Before you start • Windows 10/11 PC with virtualization enabled in BIOS/UEFI • At least 8 GB RAM and about 30 GB free disk space • A stable internet connection: the ISO is about 3 GB • About 25 minutes, most of it waiting for the download • Every screenshot in this series is from a real PC. LAB 4 ● 1 — CONCEPTS Cloning: Linked or Full Install once, then copy. A clone is a new VM made from an existing one, so ten identical lab machines cost minutes, not hours. Linked clone Full clone What it is Points to the parent's disk and stores only its own changes A complete, separate copy of the disk Disk space Very small About the size of the parent's used data Speed Seconds Longer: the disk is copied Independence Needs the parent's files to run Fully independent Best for Quick labs and tests Backups, moving, long-term use ⚠ Security: A clone inherits everything: the password, the SSH keys, the hostname, and the machine ID.
