CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Week 1: Introduction to Web Application Security Learning Objectives By the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Explain what “web application security” means and how it differs from general network security. • Trace the full connection path between a browser and a server: DNS, TCP, TLS, then HTTP — and say why each layer matters. • Distinguish between client-side and server-side attack surfaces in a web application. • Apply the CIA triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) to a web application scenario. • Explain why mixing code and data in the same input stream is the root cause of injection-class vulnerabilities. • Describe the legal and ethical framework for security testing: authorization, rules of engagement, and responsible disclosure. What is a web application? A web application is software that runs on a remote server and is accessed through a browser, Gmail, online banking, a university portal, an online store. Unlike a program installed on your laptop, none of the application's code runs permanently on your machine. Instead, your browser sends a request over the internet, the server processes it and often talks to a database behind the scenes, and it sends back a response that your browser turns into the page you see. This request/response cycle happens every time you click a link, submit a form, or load a page. How a browser and a server actually connect Before any application-level request happens, several lower layers do their job first. It's worth naming them now, because next week's lecture (HTTP Protocol Deep Dive) builds directly on this sequence: Figure 1 — Four steps happen before your browser ever "talks" to the application itself. 1 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security • DNS Resolution: the browser turns a name like example.com into an IP address. • TCP Handshake: the browser and server exchange SYN / SYN-ACK / ACK to open a reliable connection. • TLS Handshake: (for HTTPS) both sides agree on encryption keys so traffic in between can't be read or silently altered. TLS provides confidentiality and integrity for data in transit and, through certificates, authenticates the server to the client. • HTTP Request/Response: only now does the actual application conversation begin (GET /login, and so on). Web application security assumes this connection layer already happened correctly, and focuses on what occurs after it inside the HTTP conversation itself. That's exactly where next week's lecture picks up. Network security vs. web application security Network security protects the pipes: firewalls, routers, VPNs, the TLS layer you just saw. Web application security protects what runs on top of those pipes the application logic itself. A firewall won't stop an attacker who logs in through the normal front door and then manipulates a form field to see another user's data, because from the network's point of view that traffic looks completely legitimate. That's an application-layer problem, and it's what this course focuses on: not how data travels, but what the application does with it once it arrives. Figure 2 — The basic application flow. Most vulnerabilities you'll study live inside the server logic, not the wires connecting the boxes. The attack surface of a web application It helps to split where attacks actually land into two broad categories. This split will keep reappearing as a way to organize everything you learn this semester: 2 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Client-Side Attacks Server-Side Attacks (target the victim's browser) (target the app server, database, and backend services) Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) — Week 6 SQL Injection — Week 9 Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) — Week 7 Command Injection DOM-based manipulation Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Clickjacking Broken Access Control — Week 12 Client-side attacks trick the victim's own browser into doing something harmful, often without the server ever being touched directly. Server-side attacks go after the backend directly: the application server, its database, or the internal services it talks to knowing which side an attack targets helps you reason about its impact and where the fix has to go. Why web apps are attractive targets Three properties make web applications a favorite target for attackers: • They're publicly reachable. There's no need to breach an internal network first, anyone with a browser can reach the login page. • They usually hold valuable data: passwords, payment details, personal records, business data. • They're complex. More features and more code mean more places for a small mistake to hide, and a single missed check can undermine an otherwise well-built system. The CIA triad, applied to web apps Almost every security discussion, including this course, comes back to three goals: • Confidentiality: only authorized users can see the data. Your bank balance should stay private to you. • Integrity: data isn't changed without permission. No one should be able to quietly edit your order total or someone else's grade. • Availability: the service stays reachable. A flood of fake requests shouldn't be able to take the site offline for real users. 3 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Figure 3 — The CIA triad. Every attack you study this semester breaks at least one of these three goals. You'll use this triad as a lens all semester. XSS mainly threatens confidentiality by stealing session data. SQL injection can break both confidentiality and integrity at once. A denial-of-service attack targets availability specifically. The fundamental flaw: mixing code and data Almost every injection-class vulnerability: SQL Injection, Command Injection, XSS, and others you'll meet this semester traces back to one single design mistake: letting user input be interpreted as executable instructions instead of treating it purely as raw data. A safely built system always keeps a hard boundary between "this is a command" and "this is just a value." The moment that boundary blurs, whoever controls the input effectively controls part of the program's logic. Keep this one sentence in mind, it explains more of the OWASP Top 10 than any other single idea: “An interpreter that treats user input as code, instead of as data, is already broken.” A detailed example: SQL Injection Consider a login form that checks a username and password against a database. A safely written application treats whatever the user types purely as data. But if the developer builds the database query by directly pasting in the raw text the user typed, the boundary described above disappears an attacker can type something that changes the query itself, not just its value. Nothing about the network or the server's operating system was attacked here, the vulnerability lives entirely in how the application handled user input. This exact idea, 4 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security SQL Injection, is the subject of Week 9, and the same root cause reappears in XSS (Week 6), CSRF (Week 7), and several other topics this semester. Figure 4 — Same login form, two different inputs. The malicious input turns part of the query into a condition that's always true. The OWASP Top 10 — and which edition to use Different sources may show a different ranking depending on which edition they cite, so the year matters. The edition most textbooks, exam question banks, and the official OWASP documentation listed in this course's required texts are built around is the 2021 edition: • • • • • • • • • • A01:2021 – Broken Access Control A02:2021 – Cryptographic Failures A03:2021 – Injection A04:2021 – Insecure Design A05:2021 – Security Misconfiguration A06:2021 – Vulnerable and Outdated Components A07:2021 – Identification and Authentication Failures A08:2021 – Software and Data Integrity Failures A09:2021 – Security Logging and Monitoring Failures A10:2021 – Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) OWASP released an updated 2025 edition that reshuffles this ranking (for example, Security Misconfiguration jumps from #5 to #2, and Software Supply Chain Failures appears as a new category). This course will primarily reference the 2021 edition, since 5 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security it matches your required text, but when you read outside material, always check which year is being cited before comparing category numbers across sources. Legal and ethical responsibility Knowing how to find a vulnerability comes with a responsibility not to misuse that knowledge. Testing, scanning, or attempting to break into a system you don't own and don't have explicit written permission to test is illegal in most countries, regardless of good intentions: "I was just curious" is not a legal defense. Professional security work is built around three concepts you should know by name: • Rules of Engagement (RoE): a written agreement, made before testing starts, that defines exactly what is in-scope (systems you may test) and out-of-scope (everything else), plus timing, methods allowed, and points of contact. • Responsible / Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure: when you find a real flaw, you report it privately to the system's owner first, giving them a fair window (commonly around 90 days) to fix it before any public disclosure. • Safe Harbor & Bug Bounty Programs: platforms such as HackerOne and Bugcrowd let organizations publish an official, legally protected scope for researchers, so testing within that scope is authorized and (often) paid, instead of being a crime. Throughout this course, every hands-on exercise happens inside environments built specifically for practice, so you can experiment freely without legal or ethical risk. Get comfortable with this mindset now permission first, always because it's the standard you're expected to carry into your professional career. 6 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Week 2: HTTP Protocol Deep Dive Learning Objectives By the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Describe the structure of an HTTP request and response: start line, headers, and body. • Explain the common HTTP methods and when each is appropriate — and how the method itself can be tampered with. • Distinguish precisely between 401 Unauthorized (unauthenticated) and 403 Forbidden (unauthorized), and explain what status codes can leak. • Explain why HTTP is stateless, how cookies restore state, and what each SameSite value (Strict / Lax / None) actually does. • Identify key security-relevant HTTP headers, including how Referer and caching headers can leak sensitive data. • Explain how TLS turns HTTP into HTTPS, connecting back to the connection layers from Week 1. • Recognize Host Header Injection as a way HTTP's own trust assumptions get abused. Anatomy of an HTTP message Every HTTP message, request or response, has the same four-part shape: a start line, a set of headers, a blank line, and an optional body. Learn to read this shape and you can read any HTTP traffic you'll ever intercept with a tool like Burp Suite or the browser's DevTools. • • • • Start line / status line — what is being asked for (request), or what happened (response). Headers — metadata about the message: format, size, cookies, caching rules, and more. Blank line — marks the end of headers; nothing subtle here, just a required separator. Body — the actual payload: form data going up, HTML/JSON coming back down. The method states the client's intent. Two properties matter for security and correctness: whether a method is safe (doesn't change server state) and whether it's idempotent (sending the same request twice has the same effect as sending it once). 7 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Figure 1 — A request and a matching response, broken into their four parts. HTTP methods Method Purpose Safe? Idempotent? GET Retrieve a resource Yes Yes POST Create a resource / submit data No No PUT Replace a resource entirely No Yes PATCH Partially update a resource No No DELETE Remove a resource No Yes HEAD Like GET, but headers only, no body Yes Yes OPTIONS Ask what methods/headers are allowed (CORS preflight) Yes Yes One practical security consequence: GET parameters travel in the URL, which means they get written into browser history, server access logs, and proxy logs in plain sight. Never put passwords, tokens, or other secrets in a GET query string, use POST with a body instead. The method is also something an attacker can try to abuse directly. Verb tampering (or method override abuse) happens when an access-control rule only checks the literal HTTP method; for example, a firewall rule that blocks POST to /admin/delete but forgets GET or HEAD to the same path. Some frameworks also honor a header like XHTTP-Method-Override, letting a client claim a request is really a PUT or DELETE. If 8 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security the application trusts that override without re-checking permissions, an attacker can smuggle a blocked action through an allowed method. The fix is simple in principle: authorize the action, not the verb string. HTTP status codes at a glance • • • • • 1xx Informational: rare in everyday use, e.g. 100 Continue. 2xx Success: 200 OK, 201 Created. 3xx Redirection: 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found. 4xx Client Error: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found. 5xx Server Error: 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable. 401 and 403 are commonly confused, and the exact distinction is worth knowing precisely: 401 Unauthorized actually means unauthenticated, the server doesn't know who you are yet, because no valid credentials (login, token) were presented. 403 Forbidden means the opposite problem: your identity is known and confirmed, but your permissions aren't sufficient for this specific resource. In short, 401 asks "who are you?" and 403 says "I know who you are, and the answer is still no." Status codes can leak more than they should in other ways too. If a login page returns one message for "wrong password" and a different one for "no such user," an attacker can use that difference to enumerate valid usernames, one status code at a time. A welldesigned authentication endpoint returns the same generic error either way. We'll return to this exact issue in Week 3 (Authentication and Session Management). HTTP is stateless By design, HTTP treats every request as brand new: the server keeps no memory of your previous requests. That's what "stateless" means. But a login session obviously needs to persist across many requests, so the application has to manufacture that memory itself, and the standard way to do it is cookies. Three cookie attributes matter enormously for security, and you'll see all three again later this semester: • Secure: the cookie is only ever sent over HTTPS, never plain HTTP. • HttpOnly: JavaScript cannot read the cookie, which limits what a successful XSS attack (Week 6) can steal. • SameSite: restricts whether the cookie is sent along with requests coming from another site, which is a core defense against CSRF (Week 7). 9 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Figure 2 — The server has no memory of its own; the cookie the browser keeps re-sending is what creates the illusion of a continuous session. SameSite specifically takes one of three values, and the difference matters a lot once you reach CSRF in Week 7: Value Behavior Strict The cookie is never sent with any cross-site request, even a normal link click coming from another site. Strongest protection, but can break legitimate cross-site flows. Lax The cookie is sent only with "safe" top-level navigation (e.g., clicking a normal link), but not with cross-site POSTs, images, or iframes. This is the modern browser default. None The cookie is sent with every cross-site request, with no restriction. Requires the Secure flag to also be set (HTTPS only). • Domain: controls which hosts receive the cookie. • Path: restricts the URL paths where the cookie is sent. 10 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Security-relevant HTTP headers Beyond cookies, a handful of response headers let a server tell the browser to defend itself: Header What it protects against Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) Forces the browser to use HTTPS only for this site, blocks downgrade / SSL-stripping attacks. Content-Security-Policy (CSP) Restricts which scripts and resources are allowed to run on the page, a major defense against XSS (Week 6). X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff Stops the browser from guessing a file's type, closing off some content-type confusion attacks. X-Frame-Options Blocks the page from being loaded inside another site's <iframe> prevents clickjacking. Access-Control-Allow-Origin Part of CORS: controls which other origins may read this response via JavaScript (Week 14). Referrer-Policy: no-referrer Stops the browser from sending the previous page's full URL (which may contain a sensitive token or ID) to a third-party site. Data leakage through headers and caching Two everyday headers cause real-world data leaks that have nothing to do with a classic "attack", just careless defaults. The Referer header tells the next site which page you came from, including the full URL. If a sensitive URL contains a token (for example, https://app.edu/reset?token=abc123) and that page has a link or embedded image from a third-party site, the browser will happily hand that token to the third party in the Referer header. The Referrer-Policy header (shown above) is how a developer prevents that leak. Cache-Control: no-store matters for a related but different reason: it tells both the browser and any intermediate proxy never to store a copy of the response at all. Without it, a sensitive page: a bank statement, a grade report: can remain in the browser's local cache after the user logs out. On a shared or public workstation, the next person can sometimes recover that page by pressing "back" or browsing the cache directly, even though the session itself has ended. Host Header Injection The Host header tells the server which website the request is meant for, which matters when one server hosts multiple sites. The problem is that some applications trust this 11 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security client-supplied header blindly and use it to build absolute URLs: most dangerously, in password-reset emails ("click here: https://{Host}/reset?token=..."). If the app doesn't validate Host against an allow-list of its real domains, an attacker can submit a password-reset request with Host: attacker.com. The application, trusting the header, builds the reset link using that fake domain, so when the legitimate user (or an automated system) clicks it, the reset token is sent straight to the attacker. This specific abuse is known as password-reset poisoning, and the fix is simple: never build securitysensitive URLs from client-controlled input. HTTPS = HTTP + TLS HTTPS isn't a different protocol from HTTP, it's the same HTTP conversation, wrapped inside the TLS encryption layer from Week 1's connection sequence. TLS gives you three guarantees: the traffic is encrypted (confidentiality), it can't be silently altered in transit (integrity), and through the site's certificate you have some assurance you're actually talking to the real server (authenticity). That's why a browser's "connection not secure" warning should never be dismissed reflexively: it usually means one of those three guarantees just failed. 12 Ahmad Salim

p: CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Week 3: Authentication and Session Management Learning Objectives By the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Distinguish authentication from authorization, and connect that distinction to the 401/403 codes from Week 2. • Describe the three authentication factors and explain why combining them (MFA) is stronger than any one alone. • Explain how passwords must be stored (salted, slow hashing) and why plaintext or fast hashes are unacceptable. • Describe how session management works and why the session ID must be regenerated at login. • Identify common authentication attacks: brute force, credential stuffing, session hijacking, session fixation, and their mitigations. • Describe, at a high level, how token-based authentication (JWT) and OAuth/SSO differ from classic session cookies. Authentication vs. authorization These two words get used almost interchangeably in casual conversation, but they answer different questions. Authentication (AuthN) answers "who are you?" logging in with a username and password proves your identity. Authorization (AuthZ) answers "what are you allowed to do?" once your identity is known, the system decides which resources and actions are permitted for that identity. This is exactly the distinction behind Week 2's 401 vs. 403: a 401 means authentication failed (identity unknown), a 403 means authentication succeeded but authorization failed (identity known, action denied). Authentication factors An authentication factor is a category of evidence used to prove identity. Relying on just one factor almost always "something you know", is the weakest setup, which is why Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) combines factors from at least two different categories. MFA is effective because it forces an attacker to defeat two unrelated categories at once. A leaked password alone is no longer enough if the account also requires a code from your phone. 13 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Factor Examples Weakness if used alone Something you know Password, question PIN, security Can be guessed, phished, or reused from another breach. Something you have Can be lost, stolen, or (for Phone (OTP app/SMS), SMS) intercepted via SIM hardware key (YubiKey) swap. Something you are Fingerprint, recognition face Can't be "reset" if the biometric data is ever compromised. How passwords should (and shouldn't) be stored A password should never be recoverable from the database, not stored in plaintext, and not stored with reversible encryption. It should be hashed: run through a one-way function so that verifying a login means re-hashing the entered password and comparing hashes, never decrypting anything. Two more details make this actually safe: a unique random salt per user (so identical passwords don't produce identical hashes, defeating precomputed rainbow-table attacks) and a deliberately slow algorithm (so that guessing millions of passwords per second becomes computationally expensive). Figure 1 — The same breach, two different outcomes, depending entirely on how passwords were stored. 14 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security OWASP's current guidance ranks acceptable algorithms as: Argon2id first choice, scrypt as a fallback, bcrypt for legacy systems only, and PBKDF2 where FIPS-140 compliance is required. Fast general-purpose hashes like plain MD5 or SHA-256 are not acceptable for passwords, they're designed to be fast, which is exactly the wrong property here. Session management Once you're authenticated, the server issues a session ID: a long, random, unguessable value and sends it via Set-Cookie (Week 2). From then on, the browser resends that ID with every request, and the server looks it up in its session store to know who's asking. Two operational details matter: sessions should expire after a period of inactivity (an idle timeout), and critically a fresh session ID should always be issued at the moment of login, replacing whatever ID the browser held before. Skipping that second step is precisely what enables the next attack. Session Fixation In a session fixation attack, the attacker doesn't need to steal anything, they simply get the victim to authenticate using a session ID the attacker already controls. Figure 2 — The attacker never touches the victim's credentials; they only need the server to keep reusing the same session ID after login. The root cause is the same theme from Week 1 and Week 2: trusting something that should have been regenerated. The fix is one rule, applied consistently: every privilege change logging in, but also elevating to an admin role should issue a brand-new session ID. 15 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Common authentication and session attacks Attack How it works Primary mitigation Brute Force Automated tool tries many password guesses against one account. Account lockout / rate limiting, CAPTCHA, MFA. Credential Stuffing Attacker replays username/password pairs leaked from other, unrelated breaches. MFA, checking new passwords against known-breach lists, per-IP rate limiting. Session Hijacking Attacker steals a valid session ID via XSS, network sniffing on plain HTTP, or a leaked log. HttpOnly + Secure cookies (Week 2), HTTPS everywhere. Session Fixation Attacker forces the victim to authenticate while using a session ID the attacker already knows. Regenerate the session ID the moment a user logs in (see Figure 2). Modern authentication: tokens, OAuth, and SSO Classic session cookies require the server to keep a lookup table of every active session. An alternative is token-based authentication, most commonly JSON Web Tokens (JWT): a self-contained token made of three base64url-encoded parts (header.payload.signature). The header names the signing algorithm, the payload carries claims (who the user is, when the token expires), and the signature created with a server-held secret or private key lets the server verify the token wasn't tampered with, without needing to store it anywhere. This trades server-side memory for a new risk: a stolen token is valid until it expires, since there's no session store entry to revoke. OAuth 2.0 and Single Sign-On (SSO) solve a related but different problem: letting a user authenticate once with a trusted identity provider (Google, Microsoft, your university account) and reuse that identity across multiple applications, instead of creating yet another password to manage and from the application's side, avoiding the responsibility of storing passwords at all. 16 Ahmad Salim

t: Web Applications Security · L4 · Web Application Architecture
p: CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Week 4: Web Application Architecture Learning Objectives By the end of this lecture, you should be able to: • Describe the layered (N-tier) architecture of a typical web application: presentation, application, and data tiers. • Identify the components that sit around this core in production; reverse proxy, API gateway, cache, CDN, third-party services; and their individual security considerations. • Explain the MVC pattern and where input validation and business logic should live within it. • Apply the STRIDE threat-modeling framework to identify concrete threats at each architectural trust boundary. • Explain Web Cache Poisoning, Web Cache Deception, and HTTP Request Smuggling as attacks that exploit the existence of intermediary components. • Describe Zero Trust and mutual TLS (mTLS) for microservice-to-microservice traffic, and explain how SSRF exploits misplaced internal trust. • Explain database-tier privilege separation: least privilege, and splitting read and write accounts. The three classic tiers Since Week 1, our diagrams have shown three boxes: browser, server, database. That's actually a simplified version of the standard three-tier architecture: a presentation tier (what the user sees and interacts with), an application tier (the business logic that decides what to do with input), and a data tier (persistent storage). Splitting these into separate layers isn't just organizational, it's a security boundary. Code in the presentation tier should never talk to the database directly; every request has to pass through the application tier's logic first. Production Architecture Real applications add several components around this core, mostly for performance, reliability, and scale but each one changes the attack surface too. 17 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Figure 1 — A more realistic picture than "browser talks to server." Each box here is a separate piece of software with its own configuration to get right. Component Reverse Proxy Load Balancer API Gateway / Role Key security consideration Distributes traffic across servers, often terminates TLS Must forward the real client IP and handle the Host header safely (Week 2's Host Header Injection). Single entry point for backend/microservice APIs Good place to centralize auth and rate limiting, but a single misconfiguration exposes everything behind it. Application Server Executes business logic Where most injection vulnerabilities actually live. Cache (e.g. Redis) Speeds up repeated reads Can leak sensitive data across users if not access-controlled per session. Serves static assets from edge locations Cache-poisoning and cache-deception risk if misconfigured (see below). Persistent storage Should never be directly reachable from the internet; use least-privilege accounts (see below). External integrations (payments, maps, analytics...) Expands your attack surface beyond code you control; a supply-chain risk. CDN Database Third-Party APIs 18 and logic Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security The MVC pattern Within the application tier, most web frameworks organize code using Model-ViewController (MVC). The Model holds data and business rules; the View renders what the user sees; the Controller receives incoming requests, decides what should happen, and coordinates the other two. From a security standpoint, this matters because it tells you where checks belong: input validation and authorization checks belong in the Controller and Model, before any business logic runs (never left to the View), and never assumed to have already happened somewhere upstream. Trust boundaries A trust boundary is any point where data crosses from a zone you don't control into a zone you do, or from a lower-privilege context into a higher-privilege one. The browser and the network between it and your server are always untrusted, no matter how the request looks. Once inside the application tier, data is still not automatically safe for the database; it has to cross one more boundary, ideally through parameterized queries. Figure 2 — The SQL Injection example from Week 1 is exactly what happens when the boundary before the database zone is skipped. Making it concrete: applying STRIDE "Draw boundaries and check them" is easy to say and vague to act on. STRIDE gives it structure: for each boundary, ask which of six threat categories applies: Spoofing (pretending to be someone/something else), Tampering (altering data in transit or at rest), Repudiation (denying an action with no way to prove otherwise), Information Disclosure (exposing data to those who shouldn't see it), Denial of Service (making the system unavailable), and Elevation of Privilege (gaining more access than granted). Applied to Figure 1's boundaries: This is what "threat modeling" concretely means: walk the architecture diagram boundary by boundary, and for each one, ask which STRIDE category applies and what the defense is, before the system is built not after an incident. 19 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Architectural boundary Likely STRIDE threat Impact & primary defense Client → CDN / Proxy Tampering, Denial of Service Traffic altered or flooded in transit → TLS everywhere, rate limiting, a WAF. Proxy → App Server Spoofing, Information Disclosure Forged client IP or Host header (Week 2) → validate X-Forwarded-For, allow-list real domains. App Server → Database Tampering, Elevation Privilege of SQL Injection (Week 1) or an over-privileged DB account → parameterized queries + leastprivilege accounts. App Server → Other Microservices Spoofing, Elevation of Privilege Internal network wrongly assumed "safe" → mutual TLS + Zero Trust (see below). When the intermediary itself is exploited: cache attacks A CDN or cache sits between the user and your origin server specifically to avoid recomputing the same response repeatedly. That convenience creates two distinct attack classes. Web Cache Poisoning abuses "unkeyed inputs", headers or parameters that influence the response but are not part of what the cache uses to identify it, such as XForwarded-Host. If the origin reflects that header into the page and the cache key ignores it, one malicious request poisons the cached copy served to everyone else afterward. Web Cache Deception works the opposite way: instead of poisoning shared content, it tricks the cache into storing a private one. A request like /account/profile.css can hit a dynamic, authenticated endpoint that some servers still serve normally regardless of the fake static-looking extension but the cache, fooled by the .css suffix, stores that personal page as if it were a static asset, making one user's private data retrievable by anyone who requests the same URL. 20 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Figure 3 — The attacker only needs to hit the cache once; every later visitor to that same URL inherits the poisoned response. HTTP Request Smuggling: when the proxy and backend disagree Week 2 showed that a message body's length can be declared two different ways: Content-Length (a byte count) or Transfer-Encoding: chunked (a series of selfdescribing chunks). Request smuggling happens when a request includes both headers and the reverse proxy trusts one while the backend trusts the other, most classically "CL.TE", where the proxy uses Content-Length and the backend uses TransferEncoding. Figure 4 — The proxy forwards what it thinks is one complete, harmless request. The backend, parsing the same bytes differently, finds a second request hidden inside — one the proxy's security rules never inspected. 21 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security The danger is that any security filtering the proxy does (blocking /admin, for instance) only ever sees the outer request; the smuggled inner request reaches the backend having skipped that filter entirely. The fix is architectural, not a single patch: keep proxy and backend HTTP parsing strictly consistent, and prefer HTTP/2 end-to-end where the framing itself removes this ambiguity. Monolith vs. microservices A monolith runs the entire application as one deployable unit simpler to build and reason about, but a single vulnerability can potentially expose everything, sharing one blast radius. A microservices architecture splits the application into many small, independently deployed services that talk to each other over the network, limiting how far a single compromised service can reach, but multiplying the number of network boundaries that each need their own authentication and validation, exactly like the fourth row of the STRIDE table above. Securing the seams: Zero Trust and mTLS A common and dangerous assumption in microservices is that traffic from "inside the network" (localhost, the private VPC) can be trusted by default. Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) rejects that assumption outright: no request is trusted just because of where it came from — every service-to-service call is authenticated and authorized, every time. The standard mechanism is mutual TLS (mTLS): unlike ordinary HTTPS, where only the server proves its identity to the browser, mTLS has both sides present certificates, so Service A cryptographically proves who it is to Service B and vice versa. In larger deployments this is often handled by a service mesh, a dedicated infrastructure layer that automatically wraps every internal call in mTLS without each service having to implement it individually. Skipping this is exactly how Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF, OWASP A10:2021) becomes dangerous in a microservices world: if the application server will fetch any URL it's given, and internal services trust anything arriving from "inside," an attacker who tricks the app server into requesting an internal-only address can reach services that were never meant to face the internet — including, on cloud platforms, internal metadata endpoints (such as 169.254.169.254) that can hand over cloud credentials outright. Database-tier security The database deserves the same least-privilege thinking as everything else. The application should never connect as a superuser: separate accounts by function, so a bug or an injection in a read-only endpoint can't be leveraged to write or delete data. Connection pooling (reusing a small set of open database connections instead of 22 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security opening a new one per request) should be configured per account type as well, so a compromised read path can't silently borrow write-level credentials. Account Privileges Reporting pages, search, read-heavy endpoints App read account SELECT only App write account SELECT, INSERT, DROP/ALTER) Migration account / admin Used by UPDATE Full schema privileges (no Core transactional logic (checkout, profile updates) CI/CD migration jobs only — never the running application Insecure design and the OWASP Top 10 This week's theme maps to OWASP A04:2021 – Insecure Design, a category about flaws baked into the architecture itself — before a single line of vulnerable code is even written. STRIDE, applied above, is exactly the kind of threat modeling this category asks for: during design, deliberately ask "what could go wrong here, and for whom?" for every trust boundary and every component, rather than only reacting to vulnerabilities discovered after the system is built. A well-coded implementation of a badly designed architecture is still insecure. Putting it together: a booking/payment application Consider a realistic booking-and-payment app built on Figure 1's shape. The Redis cache holds session data and should sit on a private network segment, reachable only from the App Server tier — never exposed to the CDN, the browser, or the public internet directly. Payment-provider API keys and database credentials live in a secrets manager, injected into the App Server at startup, never hard-coded and never returned in any API response. The App Server itself should be explicitly forbidden from making outbound requests to internal IP ranges or cloud metadata addresses unless a specific, allow-listed feature requires it — the concrete control that prevents the SSRF scenario described above. And when the App Server calls the payment microservice internally, that call goes over mTLS, authenticated like any external request, not waved through because it happens to originate "inside." Every one of these decisions is a direct application of a rule introduced earlier in this lecture — least privilege, Zero Trust, and a trust boundary that actually gets checked. 23 Ahmad Salim

t: Web Applications Security · L5 · Securing Web Application Data
p: CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Week 5: Securing Web Application Data Learning Objectives By the end of this lecture, the student should be able to: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. Distinguish encoding, encryption, and hashing, and identify the appropriate use case for each technique. Explain the difference between protecting data in transit and protecting data at rest. Describe how symmetric and asymmetric encryption work together inside the TLS handshake introduced in Week 1. Apply data classification levels to determine which protections a given category of data requires. Explain the core principles of key management, including secure storage, rotation, and the danger of hard coded keys. Describe tokenization and data minimization as practical strategies for reducing exposure. Connect data protection failures to OWASP A02:2021, Cryptographic Failures. Continuity from Week Four Week Four examined the architecture of a web application as a chain of components, each guarded by a trust boundary. This lecture narrows the focus to one specific asset that moves through every layer of that chain: the data itself. The question addressed here is not who may access a system, but how the information inside that system is protected once an access decision has already been made. Data Classification as a Starting Point Before any protection can be applied, the data itself must be classified. A common scheme divides information into four levels: public data, meant for anyone; internal data, meant only for staff or authenticated users; confidential data, such as financial records or business plans; and restricted data, which includes personally identifiable information, health records, and payment details. The classification of a given field determines the strength of protection it requires. Treating a public marketing page and a customer's national identification number with the same level of care wastes effort in one direction and creates unnecessary risk in the other. Data classification schemes vary between organizations; the four-level model below is a simplified example used to illustrate protection requirements. 24 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Level Example Required protection Public Marketing pages, published pricing Integrity checks only; confidentiality is not a concern. Internal Internal documentation, nonpublic reports Access control and authentication. Confidential Financial records, business strategy Access control plus encryption at rest. Restricted National ID numbers, health records, payment card data Encryption at rest and in transit, strict access logging, and often a regulatory obligation. Protecting Data in Transit and at Rest Data protection is generally described along two dimensions. Data in transit is information moving across a network: between the browser and the server, or between internal services. Weeks 1 and 2 already introduced the primary defense for this dimension, TLS, which wraps the HTTP conversation in encryption so that a party observing the network traffic cannot read or alter it. Data at rest is information sitting in storage: a database, a file system, a backup, or a cache. This dimension is easy to overlook, since a system can enforce HTTPS everywhere and still store an entire customer table as plain text on disk. Both dimensions require independent protection; strength in one does not compensate for weakness in the other. Distinguishing Encoding, Encryption, and Hashing These three terms are frequently confused, and the distinction carries direct security consequences. Encoding transforms data into a different format for compatibility reasons, such as Base64. It uses no secret key and is trivially reversible by anyone, so it provides no confidentiality at all. Encryption transforms data using a secret key, so that only a party holding the correct key can reverse the transformation and recover the original value. Hashing, introduced in Week 3 for password storage, is a one-way transformation with no key and no reversal; it is used to verify integrity or to compare values without ever storing the original. A cryptographic hash by itself does not provide authenticity. 25 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Technique Reversible Requires a key Typical use Encoding Yes, by anyone No Data format compatibility, such as Base64 or URL encoding. Encryption Yes, only with the key Yes Protecting the confidentiality of data in transit or at rest. Hashing No No Password storage (Week 3) and integrity verification. Symmetric and Asymmetric Encryption in Practice Encryption itself divides into two families. Symmetric encryption uses a single shared key for both encrypting and decrypting; it is fast and well suited to large volumes of data, with AES as the standard example. Asymmetric encryption uses a mathematically linked key pair, a public key that may be shared freely and a private key that must remain secret; data encrypted with the public key can be decrypted only with the matching private key. Asymmetric operations are computationally expensive compared to symmetric ones, which is why TLS, introduced in Week 1, uses both in sequence rather than choosing one. Figure 1. The handshake phase relies on asymmetric cryptography only long enough to agree on a shared session key. Every following byte of the conversation is then protected with fast symmetric encryption. Modern TLS uses asymmetric cryptography primarily for authentication and digital signatures, while ephemeral Diffie–Hellman key exchange is used to establish shared session keys. After the handshake, symmetric cryptography protects the application data because it is much faster. 26 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Principles of Key Management An encryption scheme is only as strong as the protection around its key. Three principles recur across nearly every real-world failure in this area. First, a key must never be stored alongside the data it protects, since an attacker who steals the data would then also hold the means to read it; keys belong in a dedicated key management service or hardware security module, consistent with the secrets manager introduced in Week 4. Second, keys must be rotated on a schedule, so that a key exposed at some point in the past does not remain valid indefinitely. Third, a key must never be hard coded into source code or configuration files checked into version control, since doing so effectively publishes the key to anyone with repository access, present or future. Figure 2. The same stolen backup produces two very different outcomes, depending entirely on whether encryption at rest was applied and the key was stored separately. Figure 3. The key lifecycle. 27 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Tokenization and Data Minimization Two further strategies reduce exposure without relying purely on cryptography. Tokenization replaces a sensitive value, most commonly a payment card number, with a randomly generated token that carries no mathematical relationship to the original. The mapping between token and real value is kept in a separate, tightly controlled vault. If the application database is later breached, the attacker recovers only meaningless tokens rather than usable card numbers. Tokenization is widely used in payment systems to reduce the exposure of sensitive card data and can help organizations meet applicable compliance requirements. Data minimization addresses the same problem from a different angle: collect only the data a feature genuinely requires, and delete it once its purpose has been fulfilled. Data that was never collected, or that has already been deleted, cannot be exposed in a future breach. Cryptographic Failures in the OWASP Top Ten This week's material corresponds to OWASP A02:2021, Cryptographic Failures. The category covers transmitting sensitive data in plain text rather than over TLS, applying outdated or weak algorithms such as MD5 or DES, leaving sensitive data unencrypted at rest, storing or generating keys improperly, and relying on predictable random number generation where a cryptographically secure source was required. Nearly every item in this list is a direct violation of a principle introduced earlier in this lecture. Figure 4. Protection failure analysis. 28 Ahmad Salim

t: Web Applications Security · L6 · Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
p: CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Week 6: Cross-Site Scripting Learning Objectives By the end of this lecture, the student should be able to: • Define Cross-Site Scripting and explain why it violates the separation between code and data introduced in Week 1. • Distinguish reflected, stored, and DOM based Cross-Site Scripting. • Explain what an attacker gains by executing a script in a victim's browser, including session theft. • Apply context aware output encoding, selecting the correct encoding rule for the HTML, attribute, JavaScript, CSS, and URL contexts. • Identify the sources and sinks involved in DOM based Cross-Site Scripting when reviewing client-side JavaScript. • Explain how input validation, Content Security Policy, and HttpOnly cookies contribute additional layers of defense. • Describe how modern front-end frameworks such as React and Angular apply automatic escaping by default, and recognize the constructs that bypass this protection. • Locate Cross-Site Scripting within the OWASP Top Ten and explain why the 2021 edition merged it into the Injection category. Definition of Cross-Site Scripting Cross-Site Scripting, commonly abbreviated XSS, occurs when an application includes untrusted input in a page without properly neutralizing it, allowing that input to be interpreted by the browser as executable script rather than as plain text. The browser has no way of distinguishing a legitimate script the developer intended to send from a malicious script an attacker managed to insert; both arrive from the same trusted origin and both are executed with the same privileges. The underlying flaw is identical to the one examined in Week 1 for SQL Injection: user input crosses into a context where it is interpreted as instructions instead of as data, this time inside the browser's HTML and JavaScript engine rather than inside a database query. Three Categories of Cross-Site Scripting Cross-Site Scripting is classified according to where the malicious payload lives and how it reaches the victim. 29 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Category Where the payload lives Reflected Included in the request itself, such as a URL parameter A crafted link sent to the Not stored; exists only victim, often through for a single response phishing Stored Saved on the server, such as in a comment or a profile field Persistent; served to every visitor of the affected page No further interaction needed once the payload is posted DOM based Never reaches the server; written into the page by vulnerable client-side script Depends on the vulnerable script, often not stored Manipulating a URL fragment or another client-side input source Persistence Typical delivery Sources and Sinks in DOM Based Cross-Site Scripting DOM based Cross-Site Scripting deserves closer attention because it never touches the server at all, so server-side defenses such as output encoding on the backend cannot reach it. Reviewing client-side JavaScript for this category requires two standard terms borrowed directly from static analysis. A source is any point where untrusted data enters the script, most commonly a piece of the current URL or a value handed to the page by the browser itself. A sink is any function or property that can turn a plain string into markup that is parsed or code that is executed. A vulnerability exists precisely when a value flows from a source into a sink without passing through a safe transformation in between. Category Representative examples Sources (untrusted input reaching clientside script) location.hash, location.search, document.referrer, document.URL, window.name, and data delivered through postMessage. Sinks (constructs that turn a string into executed code or rendered markup) element.innerHTML and element.outerHTML, document.write() and document.writeln(), eval(), new Function(), setTimeout() or setInterval() when given a string argument, and an event handler attribute set directly from untrusted data. The safest response to this category is to avoid the dangerous sinks entirely wherever possible, favoring element.textContent, which always treats its argument as displayable text, or building elements explicitly through the document object model rather than assembling markup as a string. 30 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security A Detailed Walkthrough of Stored Cross-Site Scripting Stored Cross-Site Scripting is the most consequential of the three categories, since a single successful injection can affect every subsequent visitor without any further action from the attacker. Figure 1. A single malicious comment, once stored without encoding, executes inside the browser of every visitor who later views the page. The comment field in this example behaves in the same way as the login field examined in Week 1. Both accept text from an untrusted source, and both fail only at the moment that text is treated as something other than plain data. What an Attacker Gains A script running inside a victim's browser, under the victim's own authenticated session, can perform almost anything the victim could do manually. The most common objective is session theft: reading the session cookie established in Week 3 and sending it to a server the attacker controls, after which the attacker can impersonate the victim without ever knowing a password. Beyond cookie theft, the same script can capture keystrokes, redirect the page to a convincing fake login form, silently submit requests on the victim's behalf, or simply deface the page. Several of these outcomes, particularly forcing an action on the victim's behalf, reappear in Week 7 under Cross-Site Request Forgery. 31 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Output Encoding as the Primary Defense The core defense against Cross-Site Scripting mirrors the core defense against SQL Injection from Week 1: untrusted input must never be interpreted as code. In the browser, this means applying output encoding at the exact point where data is written into a page, converting characters with special meaning, such as angle brackets, into their harmless text equivalents. Figure 2. The same submitted text produces two outcomes, entirely dependent on whether the application encoded it before writing it into the page. Output context Where it appears Correct encoding rule HTML body HTML entity encoding of the characters Text placed between ordinary with special meaning, including the angle tags, such as inside a paragraph brackets, the ampersand, and the quotation or a division marks HTML attribute Entity encoding of every character outside a A value placed inside an small safe set, since an attribute can be attribute, such as a value or an closed by characters other than an angle href bracket JavaScript variable A value placed inside a script block or an inline event handler, always as an already quoted string Unicode escaping of every character, combined with never placing the value anywhere in the script other than inside an existing quoted string CSS value A value placed inside a stylesheet or a style attribute CSS hexadecimal encoding, since several CSS constructs can trigger unexpected network requests or behavior URL parameter A value placed inside a query string or another portion of a URL Percent encoding of every reserved and unsafe character 32 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Encoding must match its context. Text placed inside an HTML element requires HTML encoding; text placed inside a JavaScript block or an HTML attribute requires a different encoding scheme entirely. Applying the wrong encoding for the surrounding context leaves the application just as exposed as applying none. Five contexts account for nearly every case a developer encounters in practice. One context deserves a separate warning. Placing untrusted data directly inside a script tag, rather than inside an already quoted string within that script, is considered a dangerous context in its own right. No encoding scheme fully neutralizes this placement, since the browser's JavaScript parser interprets the surrounding structure before any encoded characters are read back as literal text. The only reliable approach is to avoid this placement altogether and pass data into scripts through a quoted variable instead. Additional Layers of Defense Output encoding is necessary but should not stand alone. Input validation restricts what a field accepts in the first place, ideally using an allow list of permitted characters or formats rather than attempting to block known malicious patterns. Where an application must accept some HTML, such as a rich text comment field, a dedicated sanitization library should parse and rebuild the markup rather than relying on custom filtering code. The Content Security Policy header, introduced in Week 2, adds a further layer that limits the damage even when an injection slips past encoding, since a strict policy can prevent inline scripts from executing and restrict which external domains a page may load script from at all. Finally, the HttpOnly cookie attribute, also introduced in Week 2, does not prevent Cross-Site Scripting from occurring, but it does prevent an injected script from directly reading the session cookie, closing off the most damaging single consequence of a successful attack. Automatic Escaping in Modern Front-End Frameworks Most applications built today do not assemble HTML by hand; they use a front-end framework such as React or Angular, and both apply automatic escaping as their default behavior. In React, a value placed inside curly braces within markup is converted to a plain string and escaped before it is written to the page, so ordinary use of the framework already applies HTML body encoding without the developer requesting it. React exposes a deliberately named escape hatch, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, for the rare case where raw markup must be rendered; the unusual name is intentional, and the framework's own documentation warns against passing user supplied content through it without an independent sanitization library. Angular follows the same philosophy through its DomSanitizer service, which automatically sanitizes values bound into HTML, style, and URL contexts, stripping dangerous constructs such as a script 33 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security element while preserving safe content. Angular likewise exposes explicit bypass methods, including bypassSecurityTrustHtml, for the case where a value has already been verified safe through other means. Neither framework eliminates XSS as a possibility. Each framework simply makes the safe behavior the default rather than something the developer must remember to apply on every output. The moment a developer reaches for an escape hatch such as dangerouslySetInnerHTML or bypassSecurityTrustHtml, responsibility shifts back onto that developer, and the same context aware encoding discipline described earlier in this lecture applies again in full. Placement Within the OWASP Top Ten In earlier editions of the OWASP Top Ten, Cross-Site Scripting stood as its own category. The 2021 edition, used as the reference throughout this course, folded it into A03:2021, Injection, alongside SQL Injection and several related weaknesses. The reasoning is direct: both vulnerabilities share the same root cause, untrusted input reaching an interpreter that cannot distinguish code from data, and differ only in which interpreter is involved, the database engine in one case and the browser's rendering engine in the other. 34 Ahmad Salim

t: Web Applications Security · L7 · Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
p: CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Week 7: Cross-Site Request Forgery Learning Objectives By the end of this lecture, the student should be able to: • Define Cross-Site Request Forgery and distinguish it from Cross-Site Scripting, examined in Week 6. • Explain the browser behavior that Cross-Site Request Forgery depends on, and describe this behavior formally as an instance of ambient authority and the confused deputy problem. • Explain why a state changing action exposed through a GET request increases exposure to this attack. • Describe the Synchronizer Token Pattern and the double submit cookie pattern, including why current guidance favors a signed, session bound variant over the naive version. • Compare the reliability of the Origin and Referer headers when verifying the declared source of a request. • Explain how the SameSite cookie attribute, introduced in Week 2, reduces exposure by default in modern browsers, and identify the specific cases, including a clicked link and a temporary browser compatibility exception, where that default still permits a forged request. • Explain why a Cross-Site Scripting vulnerability can defeat a token-based Cross-Site Request Forgery defense. • Locate Cross-Site Request Forgery within the OWASP Top Ten and explain why it is no longer treated as a standalone category. Cross-Site Request Forgery as a Failure of Ambient Authority The mechanics above are best understood through a formal concept from security theory. A subject is said to exercise ambient authority when it can perform an action on a resource merely by naming that resource, without separately presenting a specific permission scoped to that particular action. Browser cookies behave exactly this way: the browser attaches a stored cookie to a request based only on the destination domain, never checking which page or code actually initiated the request or why. This design is convenient for ordinary browsing, but it cannot distinguish an action the user meant to take from an action an unrelated page silently triggered on the user's behalf. Security literature describes this general pattern as the confused deputy problem: a program holding more authority than the party asking it to act is tricked into misusing that authority on the requester's behalf. In this scenario, the browser is the deputy, the session cookie is the authority, and the malicious page is the party that tricks the deputy into spending an authority it was never given directly. Framing the attack this way explains why token-based defenses work in principle: a token replaces implicit, ambient 35 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security authorization with an explicit, per action permission that only code running on the legitimate origin can obtain. Figure 1. The victim never leaves an authenticated session; the malicious page merely causes the browser to spend that authentication on a request the victim never intended. Risks of State-Changing GET Requests Week 2 established that GET requests are expected to be safe, meaning they should not alter server-side state. Cross-Site Request Forgery is one of the clearest illustrations of why that expectation matters in practice. A forged GET request needs nothing more elaborate than an ordinary image tag or a link pointing at the target endpoint; the browser issues the request the moment the tag is parsed, with no script and no user interaction required. A forged POST request at least requires an automatically submitting form, a small extra step for the attacker but still trivial to construct. An application that exposes a state changing action, such as a funds transfer or a password change, through a GET request has removed even that minor obstacle. Primary Defenses No single defense below is complete on its own. Effective protection typically layers a token-based defense with the SameSite cookie attribute, treating the cookie attribute as a broad safety net and the token as the mechanism that holds even when the safety net does not apply. 36 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Defense Mechanism Primary limitation Synchronizer Token Pattern The server generates a unique, unpredictable token per session, embeds Requires server-side state and it in every state changing form, and must be included in every form or rejects any submission whose token does API call. not match. Double submit cookie A random value is set as a cookie and must also be repeated as a request parameter. An attacker on another origin cannot read the cookie in order to copy the value. The plain version is weaker unless the value is signed and bound to the session, as recommended in current guidance. Custom request header Client-side script adds a custom header to state changing requests. Only script running on the same origin is permitted to set it. Not usable for a plain form submission or a followed link, only for requests made through script. SameSite cookie attribute Instructs the browser to withhold the cookie on most cross-site requests, removing the ambient authority the attack depends on. The Lax setting, the modern default, still allows the cookie on a top-level navigation such as a clicked link. Origin or Referer verification The server compares the declared source of the request against its own origin and rejects a mismatch. The Referer header can be withheld by a strict Referrer Policy, covered in Week 2, leaving nothing to compare. Figure 2. A valid session cookie is necessary but no longer sufficient once the endpoint also requires a token the forged request cannot supply. 37 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Strengthening the Double Submit Cookie Pattern The double submit cookie pattern described above is often called the naive variant, and it assumes an attacker cannot set cookies on the target domain. That assumption does not always hold. A vulnerable subdomain, an abandoned DNS record that enables a subdomain takeover, or a connection still reachable over plain HTTP can each allow an attacker to write a cookie that matches the value the application expects, defeating the comparison entirely. Current OWASP guidance therefore recommends a signed double submit cookie instead, in which the value is generated with a server-side secret through an HMAC construction and explicitly bound to the user's authenticated session identifier. An attacker who manages to set an arbitrary cookie still cannot produce a value that passes the signature check without knowing the server's secret key, closing the gap the naive version leaves open. Comparing the Origin and Referer Headers The Origin and Referer headers serve a similar verification purpose but differ in reliability. The Origin header is included in every cross-origin request and, in current browsers, in same origin POST, PUT, and DELETE requests as well; it reports only the scheme, host, and port of the requesting page, never the path, which keeps it compact and avoids leaking browsing details unnecessarily. The Referer header, by contrast, carries the full URL of the requesting page and can be suppressed entirely by a strict Referrer Policy, the header introduced in Week 2, or withheld by privacy focused browser settings. For this reason, current guidance treats the Origin header as the more dependable signal when it is present, falling back to Referer only when Origin is absent. Limitations of the SameSite Default in Practice The SameSite attribute defaulting to Lax, in effect in major browsers since 2020, blocks the cookie on most cross-site requests but was deliberately designed to still permit it on a top-level navigation performed through a GET request, such as a link the victim clicks, since blocking that case would break ordinary cross site linking across the web. A forged GET based request therefore still succeeds under the default setting, which is exactly why the earlier discussion of state changing GET requests in this lecture matters in practice and not only in principle. Chromium based browsers additionally ship a temporary compatibility exception that allows a cookie no more than two minutes old to accompany a top-level cross site POST request, added to avoid breaking certain identity federation and single sign on flows that depend on a cross-site POST shortly after a cookie is set. Browser vendors have described this exception as temporary and expected to be removed. None of these details change the central guidance of this lecture: the SameSite attribute is a valuable default, not a substitute for an explicit token. 38 Ahmad Salim

CSTE4107 – Web Applications Security Interaction Between XSS and Token-Based Defenses A Cross-Site Request Forgery token assumes that the attacker's page cannot read anything belonging to the target site. A Cross-Site Scripting vulnerability on that same site breaks this assumption directly, since injected script runs with the full privileges of the page, including the ability to read a token embedded in the page or stored in a cookie the script can access. Once the token can be read, it can simply be copied into the forged request, and the defense examined in this lecture no longer holds. This is the clearest practical link between the two lectures: a Cross-Site Scripting flaw does not just endanger the page it appears on; it can quietly remove the protection the application was relying on against an entirely different attack. Placement Within the OWASP Top Ten Cross-Site Request Forgery ranked fifth in the 2007 edition of the OWASP Top Ten and eighth in the 2013 edition, then dropped out of the list entirely starting with the 2017 edition. OWASP cited a declining incidence rate together with the fact that most modern web frameworks had begun including built in protections against it. The 2021 edition, used as the reference throughout this course, does not list Cross-Site Request Forgery as its own category, but the underlying weakness, catalogued as CWE-352, is explicitly included under A01:2021, Broken Access Control. That placement reflects the nature of the flaw accurately: an application that processes a state changing request without verifying that the request reflects the genuine intent of an authorized user has failed to control access to that action, regardless of whether the session cookie presented was valid. 39 Ahmad Salim
