p: LECTURE 1 Application Security This lecture introduces application security as the discipline of protecting software throughout its life cycle. It begins by positioning application security within the wider field of cybersecurity and explaining the shift-left principle, and then presents the core security objectives, the environments in which applications run, and the models, frameworks, and design principles that structure an application security program. Threat modeling is then developed in depth, covering data flow diagrams, trust boundaries, STRIDE, and risk ranking, and is applied in a worked example. The chapter closes with a set of secure coding practices. IN THIS LECTURE 1.1 1.2 1.3 1.4 1.5 1.6 1.7 1.8 Overview of Application Security Security Objectives of an Application Application Security Administration Application Security Models Security Frameworks and Standards Threat Modeling Worked Example: QuickBite Threat Model Secure Coding Practices 1.1 Overview of Application Security Cybersecurity is the broad discipline that protects digital systems and information. It encompasses network security, infrastructure security, and physical security, among other areas. Application security is a specific subset of cybersecurity, focused exclusively on securing software. This specialized focus involves identifying and mitigating risks that could allow unauthorized access, data theft, or system disruption. Application security is the set of measures and practices designed to protect software applications from threats and vulnerabilities throughout their life cycle. It aims to ensure that applications operate securely, safeguarding their integrity, confidentiality, and availability. Although the security domains are interconnected and may share certain controls and practices, each addresses a different layer of the broader technology environment. Establishing the position of application security within this landscape, and distinguishing it from the other domains, provides an important foundation for understanding the secure coding practices discussed later in this chapter. Table 1.1 compares the four domains according to the layer they protect and the primary mechanisms commonly used to secure it. As the comparison shows, application security has a distinct focus: it protects the software itself, including its architecture, source code, third-party 1

Chapter 1 | Application Security dependencies, and behavior during execution. This differentiates it from security disciplines that primarily address the surrounding network, computing infrastructure, or physical environment. Table 1.1 Domains of cybersecurity and their focus areas Area What it protects Typical measures Network security Traffic and connections between systems Firewalls, segmentation, intrusion detection, VPNs Infrastructure / cloud security Servers, containers, virtual machines, cloud accounts Hardening, host patching, identity and access management, configuration baselines Physical security Buildings, data centers, devices Access badges, locks, cameras Application security The software itself: its design, code, dependencies, and runtime behavior Threat modeling, secure coding, code review, SAST/DAST, dependency scanning, application monitoring 1.2 Security Objectives of an Application Application security is fundamentally concerned with protecting information and functionality. Three classical security objectives provide the foundation for this protection: confidentiality, integrity, and availability, commonly abbreviated as the CIA triad. 1.2.1 Confidentiality Confidentiality means that data is accessible only to authorized parties. When confidentiality is breached, unauthorized individuals can read data they should not see. EXAMPLE A healthcare application stores patient records. If an attacker can access those records without authorization, confidentiality is breached. This is not just a technical failure; it is a legal violation under regulations such as HIPAA. Typical failures: missing access controls, unencrypted data at rest or in transit, verbose error messages that leak information, and insecure direct object references. 1.2.2 Integrity Integrity means that data cannot be modified by unauthorized parties. When integrity is breached, data becomes unreliable, because it may have been altered without detection. EXAMPLE A banking application allows funds transfers. If an attacker can modify the amount of a transfer after it is submitted, integrity is breached and the bank’s records no longer reflect reality. Typical failures: missing input validation, lack of digital signatures, insufficient audit trails, and SQL injection that modifies database records. 2

Chapter 1 | Application Security 1.2.3 Availability Availability means that the application and its data are accessible when legitimate users need them. When availability is breached, the application becomes unusable. EXAMPLE An e-commerce platform is operating during a holiday sale. If an attacker floods the site with requests and takes it offline, availability is breached. The business loses revenue, and customers lose trust. Typical failures: denial-of-service attacks, resource exhaustion, unpatched systems that crash under load, and inadequate infrastructure capacity. 1.2.4 Authentication, Authorization, and Accountability Although the CIA triad provides the fundamental security objectives, modern applications also require mechanisms for authentication, authorization, and accountability. Authentication determines who a user, service, or system is. Authorization determines what an authenticated identity is permitted to do. Accountability provides evidence of actions performed within the system, supported by audit trails, logging, timestamps, and appropriate protection of security records. 1.2.4.1 Authentication Authentication means verifying that a user, device, or system actually is who it claims to be, before any data or functionality is made available. When authentication is weak, an attacker can step into a legitimate identity without ever needing to break confidentiality or integrity controls directly. EXAMPLE A hospital’s electronic health record (EHR) system requires clinicians to log in with a smart card and a PIN before viewing any patient data. If an attacker guesses a weak password or reuses a credential stolen from another, unrelated breach, the system may authenticate the impostor as if they were the legitimate clinician. Authentication failures do not disclose data by themselves; they simply open the door that authorization and encryption controls must then still hold. Typical failures: weak or reused passwords, no multi-factor authentication, predictable or longlived session tokens, and insecure credential storage. 1.2.4.2 Authorization Authorization means determining what an already-authenticated identity is actually permitted to do or see. Authentication and authorization are frequently confused, but a system can 3

Chapter 1 | Application Security authenticate someone correctly and still fail catastrophically if it does not then check what that person is allowed to access. EXAMPLE In a multi-tenant SaaS billing platform, a logged-in customer-support agent should be able to view invoices only for the customers assigned to them, not the invoices of every company on the platform. If the application checks merely that the requester is authenticated, rather than that they are authorized for that specific tenant’s data, any support agent could view every customer’s invoices simply by changing an account ID in the URL or API request. Typical failures: missing object-level authorization checks, relying on hidden buttons or menus instead of server-side checks, and overly broad roles that grant more access than a job function requires. 1.2.4.3 Accountability Accountability means that the system can provide trustworthy evidence of who performed a given action and when, so that events can be reconstructed and individuals cannot plausibly deny their own actions. EXAMPLE A cloud administrator deletes a production database at 2 a.m. If the platform’s audit log records only that “a delete operation occurred,” without capturing which authenticated identity performed it, from which IP address, and at what time, the organization cannot determine who was responsible or whether the action was even authorized. Accountability failures make incident response and any subsequent legal or disciplinary action nearly impossible, even when confidentiality, integrity, and availability were never directly attacked. Typical failures: missing or incomplete audit logs, logs that lack timestamps or user identifiers, logs stored on a system an attacker could compromise, and no protection against log tampering or deletion. Table 1.2 summarizes the six security objectives, the core question each one answers, and the mechanisms that primarily support it. Table 1.2 Security objectives and the mechanisms that primarily support them Objective / property Core question Representative mechanisms Confidentiality Can an unauthorized party read this information? Encryption, access control, data classification Integrity Can this information or behavior be changed without authorization? Input validation, digital signatures, audit trails Availability Can legitimate users reach the application when they need it? Rate limiting, redundancy, capacity planning Authentication Who are you? Passwords, multi-factor authentication, certificates Authorization What are you allowed to do? Role-based access control, policy engines Accountability Can we prove who did what, and when? Audit logging, timestamps, correlation identifiers 4

Chapter 1 | Application Security 1.3 Application Security Administration Technical security controls alone do not create an effective application security program. Organizations also require appropriate people, processes, and technology: three interconnected pillars that together turn individual security practices into a repeatable program (Table 1.3). Table 1.3 The three pillars of application security administration Pillar Role in the program Representative examples People Establish responsibility and make security decisions Developers, security engineers, security architects, Security Advocate, application owners Process Establish how security activities are performed consistently Threat modeling, code review, vulnerability management, patch management, incident response Technology Provide automated and technical detection mechanisms SAST, DAST, SCA, secrets scanning, runtime monitoring, CI/CD security controls 1.4 Application Security Models Several complementary models describe how organizations structure their application security efforts in practice (Table 1.4). These models are not mutually exclusive; mature organizations typically blend elements of several. Table 1.4 Application security models Model Core idea Representative controls Zero-Trust Security Eliminate implicit trust; access is continuously evaluated rather than granted because a request came from inside the network Strong identity verification, service-toservice authentication, signed tokens, just-in-time privileges Shift-Left Security Move security activities earlier in the life cycle so feedback arrives while the code is still fresh SAST in the IDE and pull request, dependency analysis, secrets scanning, automated pre-merge testing Defense in Depth Use multiple independent layers so no single control failure causes complete compromise Input validation + parameterized queries + least-privilege database accounts + authorization + monitoring DevSecOps Integrate security into existing development and operations workflows rather than a separate final stage Security findings tracked in the same issue tracker and CI/CD pipeline as other engineering work Risk-Based Security Prioritize remediation using business context rather than technical severity alone Scoring by asset criticality, data sensitivity, exploitability, and runtime exposure Note. A vulnerability’s technical severity alone often does not provide enough information to determine remediation priority; risk-based security supplies the missing business context. 5

Chapter 1 | Application Security 1.5 Security Frameworks and Standards Frameworks provide structure and common terminology for application security programs, so that organizations do not need to invent controls from scratch. Table 1.5 lists the frameworks and standards most commonly used. Table 1.5 Application security frameworks and standards Framework Publisher Primary focus OWASP (Top 10 / ASVS) Open Worldwide Application Security Project Community-maintained catalog of common risks (Top 10) and a detailed verification standard (ASVS) NIST SSDF (SP 800218) U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology Secure practices organized into four groups: Prepare, Protect, Produce, and Respond ISO/IEC 27034 International Organization for Standardization Application security management integrated into an organization’s broader information security program CIS Controls Center for Internet Security Prioritized, prescriptive safeguards spanning asset management, access control, and configuration PCI DSS PCI Security Standards Council Mandatory controls for any system that stores, processes, or transmits payment card data Note. The appropriate framework depends on the organization’s architecture, business requirements, regulatory environment, and security objectives; most mature programs draw on more than one. 1.6 Threat Modeling Threat modeling is a systematic security-analysis process used to identify, understand, prioritize, and mitigate threats to an information system before and throughout its implementation. Its fundamental purpose is to shift security analysis from a purely reactive activity, discovering vulnerabilities after a system has been developed, to a proactive activity in which potential attacks and their consequences are considered during system design. A vulnerability describes a weakness in a system; a threat describes a potential action or event that could exploit a weakness or otherwise cause harm; and risk reflects the potential consequences of that threat in the context of the system. Threat modeling connects these concepts by examining how a system operates, what it is intended to protect, who interacts with it, which components communicate, where information is stored and transmitted, and where trust relationships change. A threat-modeling process can be organized around three fundamental questions: 1. What are we building? Identify the system’s components, users, assets, data flows, external dependencies, and trust boundaries. 2. What can go wrong? Systematically identify threats that could compromise confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication, authorization, or accountability. 6

Chapter 1 | Application Security 3. What are we going to do about it? Select appropriate preventive, detective, and corrective security controls and determine how residual risk will be managed. These questions establish threat modeling as an iterative engineering activity rather than a onetime documentation exercise. 1.6.1 Data Flow Diagrams A Data Flow Diagram (DFD) provides a structured representation of how information moves through an application or system. In security-oriented threat modeling, the DFD is not merely a functional diagram. It is an analytical model that exposes the components, interactions, data stores, and trust relationships that may become relevant to an attack. A security-oriented DFD normally represents four major types of element: 1. External entities: users, external applications, organizations, devices, or third-party services that interact with the system. 2. Processes: application components or services that receive, transform, validate, or generate information. 3. Data stores: databases, files, caches, local storage, message queues, backups, or other locations where information is retained. 4. Data flows: communications or exchanges of information between entities, processes, and data stores. A fifth concept, the trust boundary, is particularly important for security analysis and is discussed next. 1.6.2 Trust Boundaries A trust boundary is a logical boundary across which the level of trust, privilege, control, or security assurance changes. It does not necessarily correspond to a physical network boundary. A trust boundary may exist between an Internet user and an internal server, between a mobile application and a backend API, between two microservices with different privileges, or between an application and a third-party service. Whenever information crosses a trust boundary, the receiving component should not automatically assume that the sender or the transmitted information is trustworthy. For example, consider a mobile banking application: Mobile User → Mobile Application → Authentication API → Banking API → Database The mobile device should generally be treated as an untrusted environment from the perspective of the backend. An attacker who controls or compromises the device may be able to inspect application files, manipulate local data, alter requests, replay communications, or instrument application execution. Consequently, security-critical decisions must not depend exclusively on controls implemented within the client application. A mobile application may provide a user interface and perform client-side validation, but the server must independently authenticate users, authorize operations, validate input, and enforce security policies. 7

Chapter 1 | Application Security At every trust boundary, the threat analyst should ask: • Who can communicate with the receiving component? • What information crosses the boundary, and is the communication authenticated? • Is the information protected in transit? • Can the sender be trusted to provide accurate information? • Can the transmitted information be modified or replayed? • Does the receiving component independently validate the information? • What happens if the communicating component becomes unavailable? • What privileges are granted after the information crosses the boundary? These questions transform a functional architecture diagram into a security-oriented representation of the system. 1.6.3 Threat Identification Using STRIDE Once the DFD has been constructed, the analyst can systematically examine its components and data flows for potential threats. One of the most widely used approaches for this purpose is STRIDE, a threat-modeling framework developed at Microsoft. STRIDE organizes threats into six categories, each corresponding to a different security property that may be violated (Table 1.7). Table 1.7 The STRIDE threat categories with definitions, examples, and typical controls STRIDE category Definition Spoofing An attacker pretends to be another user, device, service, or system component. Tampering Unauthorized modification of data, requests, configurations, or software, whether stored or in transit. Repudiation An individual or system denies having performed an action, and the system lacks trustworthy evidence of what happened. Information Disclosure Sensitive information becomes accessible to an unauthorized individual, process, or system. Security property violated Examples Typical controls Authentication / authenticity Using stolen usernames and passwords; using a stolen authentication token; impersonating an internal service; presenting a fraudulent identity to an API. Multi-factor authentication; secure credential management; secure session management; token validation; device or service authentication. Integrity Changing a transaction amount in a request (amount=100 to amount=10000); altering stored records or configurations; changing data in transit between client and server. Authenticated and encrypted communication; server-side input validation; digital signatures; access controls; database integrity constraints. Accountability / non-repudiation A customer disputes a transaction they initiated; an administrator denies a configuration change; an action cannot be traced to an authenticated identity. Secure audit logging; reliable timestamps; transaction identifiers; recording the authenticated identity; tamper-resistant logs. Confidentiality Exposure of customer records; insecure local storage of authentication tokens; excessive detail in error messages; sensitive data in logs; improperly protected backups. Encryption in transit and at rest; access control; least privilege; secure secrets management; data minimization; appropriate error handling. 8

Chapter 1 | Application Security STRIDE category Definition An attacker or failure condition prevents legitimate users from accessing a service or significantly degrades its performance. Denial of Service An attacker obtains permissions beyond those legitimately assigned to them. Elevation of Privilege Security property violated Examples Typical controls Availability Flooding a login endpoint with requests; exhausting server memory or CPU; overwhelming a database connection pool; sending excessively large requests. Rate limiting; resource quotas; request-size limits; load balancing; DDoS protection; capacity planning; monitoring and alerting. Authorization Changing an identifier to access another user’s data (/account?id=1001 to /account?id=1002); invoking administrative functions as a normal user; bypassing role checks that exist only in the client. Server-side authorization checks; role- or attributebased access control; least privilege; separation of duties; object-level authorization. 1.6.4 Threat Prioritization and Risk Ranking A threat model may identify many threats, but security teams rarely have the resources to address all of them at once, so the threats must be prioritized. A practical and transparent approach is to rate each threat on two separate dimensions: likelihood, meaning how easy or probable it is for the threat to occur, and impact, meaning how serious the consequences would be if it did. Both are rated against consistent criteria, for which the simple three-level scale in Table 1.8 can be used. Table 1.8 Three attack levels for likelihood and impact Level Likelihood Impact High (3) Requires little specialized skill or access; readily available tools or techniques exist Could affect many users, cause significant financial loss, expose sensitive information, or create safety consequences Medium (2) Requires some skill, privileged access, or specific conditions Could affect an individual or limited group, or cause moderate financial or reputational damage Low (1) Requires advanced skill, rare access, or multiple conditions to align Causes minor, temporary, or easily reversible harm SCORIN G F ORMUL A Risk Score = Likelihood × Impact The score ranges from 1 to 9. A higher score generally indicates that a threat should be addressed sooner. Table 1.9 shows the resulting scores for every combination of likelihood and impact. Table 1.9 Risk score matrix Likelihood Impact Low (1) Medium (2) High (3) High (3) 3 6 9 Medium (2) 2 4 6 9

Chapter 1 | Application Security Likelihood Impact Low (1) Low (1) Medium (2) High (3) 1 2 3 A common error in threat assessment is to confuse the two dimensions. A compromise of an entire customer database has very high impact, but that does not make it highly likely; likelihood depends on the conditions needed to carry out the attack. Likewise, a technically sophisticated attack should not automatically outrank a simple one, since an attack that needs little skill but can be repeated against thousands of users may be the greater practical risk. Good practice also avoids rating everything as High and requires a written reason for each rating. 1.7 Worked Example: QuickBite Threat Model This section applies the techniques introduced in Section 1.6 to a realistic system. The scenario is presented first, followed by 3 tasks and a model solution to each. 1.7.1 Scenario You are the security engineer for QuickBite, a food delivery app. The system works as follows: • Customers use a mobile app to browse restaurants, place orders, and pay by card. • Restaurants use a web dashboard to accept orders and update menus and prices. • Drivers use a driver app that shows pickup and drop-off addresses and shares live GPS location. • A backend API connects everyone, with a database of user profiles, addresses, and order history. • A third-party payment provider handles card payments. • A promo code system gives discounts and refunds. 1.7.2 Tasks 1. Draw a data flow diagram. Show all actors, components, data stores, and data flows. Mark at least three trust boundaries. 2. Apply STRIDE. Identify at least two realistic threats per STRIDE category (12 or more in total). Each threat must name the affected component or data flow. 3. Rank the threats. Rate each one High, Medium, or Low for likelihood and impact, calculate the score (Likelihood × Impact), and select the top five using the scale in Section 1.6.4. 10

Chapter 1 | Application Security 1.7.3 Solution to Task 1: Data Flow Diagram Figure 1.1 shows the QuickBite system with its three trust boundaries and seven numbered data flows. Figure 1.1 QuickBite data flow diagram with three trust boundaries The three trust boundaries are: • TB1, internet to QuickBite cloud: all three client devices (customer, restaurant, driver) are outside the company’s control, so everything crossing this line is untrusted input. • TB2, QuickBite to payment provider: a different organization with its own security. Messages must be authenticated in both directions. • TB3, application tier to data tier: the database holds the most sensitive data and should accept requests only from known services with minimal rights. The driver’s GPS stream (flow 3) is shown explicitly because it is easy to forget, yet it is both personal data and a business-critical signal. 1.7.4 Solution to Task 2: STRIDE Threat Register Each STRIDE category has at least two threats, and each names the component or flow affected (Table 1.10). Table 1.10 QuickBite STRIDE threat register ID Category Component / flow Threat S1 Spoofing Flow 1 / Customer login / Backend API Attacker uses credential stuffing or a stolen session token to log in as a customer, view saved addresses, and place orders on their saved card. S2 Spoofing Flows 2 and 3 / Restaurant and driver onboarding A fake restaurant or fake driver account is registered to collect orders, harvest customer addresses or phone numbers, or divert payouts. 11

Chapter 1 | Application Security ID Category Component / flow Threat T1 Tampering Flow 1 / order request Customer edits the request to change item price, delivery fee, or discount (e.g. price=12.00 becomes price=0.10) and the server trusts the values. T2 Tampering Flow 3 / driver GPS and status A rooted driver phone sends spoofed GPS coordinates or a forged “delivered” status to collect pay without delivering. T3 Tampering Flow 5 / Payment A tampered client marks an order as “paid” without a verified payment confirmation from the provider. R1 Repudiation Flows 1 and 3 / Order delivery Customer claims “my order never arrived” while the driver claims it was delivered. No proof of delivery (photo, PIN, signed event) exists. R2 Repudiation Flow 4 / Promo / refund service A support agent or restaurant user issues refunds or changes menu prices, then denies it. Admin actions are not logged with identity and time. I1 Information disclosure Flow 3 / driver app The driver app receives the customer’s full profile (phone, email, history) and keeps it after delivery, so a malicious driver can misuse it. I2 Information disclosure Flow 1 / Backend API: order history IDOR flaw: changing /orders/5521 to /orders/5522 returns another customer’s address, items, and phone number. I3 Information disclosure Flows 6 and 7 / Database: backups An unencrypted database backup or over-broad DB account leaks addresses and order history if the storage is exposed. D1 Denial of service Flow 2 / Restaurant dashboard Attacker or competitor floods a restaurant with fake orders so real customers are blocked and the restaurant must close. D2 Denial of service Flows 1 and 4 / Backend API: login and promo endpoint A bot floods the API (or brute-forces promo codes) at dinner peak, exhausting capacity so real users cannot order. E1 Elevation of privilege Flow 1 / Backend API: function-level access A customer calls restaurant-only endpoints (edit menu) because the server checks login but not role. E2 Elevation of privilege Flow 4 / Promo / refund service A driver or customer reaches the internal refund endpoint, or a support agent grants themselves admin rights, and issues unlimited refunds. 1.7.5 Solution to Task 3: Risk Ranking The scoring rule is Score = Likelihood × Impact, where High = 3, Medium = 2, and Low = 1 (maximum 9). When scores are equal, the tie-break order is as follows: the threat that puts personal safety at risk ranks higher, then the one that affects more users, then the one that costs more money. Affects more users means the number of people who would suffer real harm, such as loss of money, privacy, or account access, if the attack succeeded. Harm to the business alone 12

Chapter 1 | Application Security does not count at this step; it is covered by the cost criterion. The ranked register is given in Table 1.11. Table 1.11 QuickBite threats ranked by risk score ID Threat Likelihood Impact Score Priority rank I2 IDOR leaks other customers’ data High High 9 1 S1 Account takeover (credential stuffing) High High 9 2 T1 Price / discount tampering High High 9 3 E1 Customer calls restaurant/admin endpoints Medium High 6 4 D2 API / promo flooding at peak time High Medium 6 5 T3 Order marked paid without verified payment Medium High 6 6 E2 Refund service abused Medium High 6 7 S2 Fake restaurant / driver accounts Medium Medium 4 8 I1 Driver keeps customer data Medium Medium 4 9 D1 Fake-order flooding of a restaurant Medium Medium 4 10 T2 Spoofed GPS / forged delivery status Medium Medium 4 11 R1 No proof of delivery Medium Medium 4 12 I3 Database or backup exposure Low High 3 13 R2 Admin actions not logged Low Medium 2 14 The top five threats are I2, S1, T1, E1, and D2. Why this order. I2 ranks first among the three threats scoring 9 because it is the only one treated as a personal-safety risk: an attacker with an ordinary account of their own can change an order ID and collect the home addresses and phone numbers of thousands of other customers, without needing anyone else’s login. S1 and T1 tie on personal safety, because the main harm of S1 is financial: the attacker spends from the victim’s saved card and sees only that one account’s details, not a bulk collection of other customers’ addresses. The second criterion therefore decides between them. S1 ranks second because every hijacked account has a real victim who loses control of their account and saved card, and whose saved address is visible to the attacker. T1 ranks third because its harm falls mainly on the business, so it ranks below S1 at the usersaffected step. Among the threats scoring 6, E1 and D2 harm customers and restaurant owners across the platform, so they rank above T3 and E2 at the users-affected step. E1 and D2 tie on personal safety and users affected, so cost decides: E1 ranks above D2 because an attacker who can edit the menu causes lasting financial damage, whereas a flood causes a temporary outage. T3 and E2 tie on personal safety, because neither exposes personal data, and on users affected, because both harm mainly the business. The cost criterion does not clearly separate them, so T3 is placed first by judgment, because a payment bypass loses the full value of every order it is applied to. 13

Chapter 1 | Application Security 1.8 Secure Coding Practices Secure coding means writing software so that attackers cannot misuse it, by avoiding the common mistakes that create vulnerabilities. This section presents twelve practices. Each has a short definition and an example, with a “bad versus good” comparison where it helps. 1.8.1 Input Validation DEF IN ITIO N Never trust data from users, files, or APIs. Check that it has the expected type, length, format, and range before using it. # Bad: accepts anything age = request.form["age"] # Good: validate type and range age = int(request.form["age"]) if not (0 < age < 120): raise ValueError("Invalid age") Prefer allow-lists (accept only known-good values) over block-lists (reject known-bad values). 1.8.2 Parameterized Queries (Preventing SQL Injection) DEF IN ITIO N Keep SQL code separate from user data, so that input can never change the meaning of the query. # Bad: attacker enters ' OR '1'='1 query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'" # Good: placeholder treats input as data only cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s", (name,)) 1.10.3 Output Encoding (Preventing XSS) DEF IN ITIO N Convert special characters in user-provided data before displaying it, so that the browser shows it as text instead of running it as code. import html # Input: <script>stealCookies()</script> safe = html.escape(user_comment) # Output shown: <script>stealCookies()</script> 1.8.4 Secure Password Storage DEF IN ITIO N Never store passwords in plain text. Store a salted hash made with a slow algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2. 14

Chapter 1 | Application Security import bcrypt hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt()) bcrypt.checkpw(password.encode(), hashed) # verify at login Never use MD5 or SHA-1 for passwords. 1.10.5 Authentication and Session Management DEF IN ITIO N Reliably verify who the user is, and protect their login session afterwards. Examples: • Use multi-factor authentication (MFA). • Lock or slow down accounts after repeated failed logins. • Use random session IDs, set cookies with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite, and expire sessions after inactivity. 1.8.6 Authorization and Least Privilege DEF IN ITIO N Check what a user is allowed to do on every request, and give users and programs only the minimum permissions they need. # Bad: any logged-in user can view any invoice invoice = get_invoice(invoice_id) # Good: verify ownership invoice = get_invoice(invoice_id) if invoice.owner_id != current_user.id: abort(403) As an example of least privilege, a web application’s database account should not have permission to DROP TABLE. 1.8.7 Secrets Management DEF IN ITIO N Never hard-code passwords, API keys, or tokens in source code, and never commit them to Git. # Bad API_KEY = "sk-12345-secret" # Good: load from environment or a secrets manager import os API_KEY = os.environ["API_KEY"] 15

Chapter 1 | Application Security 1.8.8 Secure Error Handling and Logging DEF IN ITIO N Show users generic error messages, and record the details in protected logs. Never log sensitive data. # Bad: leaks internals to the user return str(exception) # "Table 'users' not found at db.py line 42" # Good logger.error("DB error", exc_info=True) # detailed, internal only return "Something went wrong. Please try again." 1.8.9 Encryption in Transit and at Rest DEF IN ITIO N Protect data while it travels (HTTPS/TLS) and while it is stored (disk or database encryption). Examples: force HTTPS everywhere, encrypt sensitive database fields, and use well-tested libraries. Never invent your own encryption algorithm. 1.8.10 Secure Defaults and Fail-Safe Design DEF IN ITIO N The system should be secure out of the box, and when something fails, it should fail closed (deny access) instead of open. # Bad: if the check crashes, access is granted try: allowed = check_permission(user) except Exception: allowed = True # Good: fail closed try: allowed = check_permission(user) except Exception: allowed = False 1.8.11 Code Review and Security Testing DEF IN ITIO N Find vulnerabilities before attackers do. Examples: peer code reviews, static analysis (SAST) tools such as Bandit or SonarQube, dynamic testing (DAST), and penetration testing. 16

Chapter 1 | Application Security 1.8.12 CSRF Protection DEF IN ITIO N Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) is an attack that tricks a logged-in user’s browser into sending an unwanted request to a website they trust. The browser automatically attaches the user’s cookies, so the server thinks the request is genuine. A simple analogy: imagine your bank honors any signed cheque that arrives with your stamp on it. An attacker cannot forge your stamp, but they can trick you into carrying their cheque to the bank yourself. 17

p: LECTURE 2 Application Security Testing (AST) Application Security Testing (AST) is the process of making applications resilient against cyber threats by identifying, analyzing, and fixing security vulnerabilities. This lecture covers the two primary strategies used in modern DevSecOps pipelines: SAST Static Application Security Testing (SAST): An inside-out, white-box testing approach that analyzes source code at rest without executing it. DAS T Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST): An outside-in, black-box testing approach that evaluates a running application by simulating real-world attacks against its endpoints. IN THIS LECTURE 2.1 2.2 Static Application Security Testing (SAST) Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) 2.1 Static Application Security Testing (SAST) SAST tools integrate early in the Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC). They scan source files, build scripts, and configurations to catch structural flaws (e.g., weak crypto, hardcoded secrets, unprotected logic patterns) before the application is compiled or deployed. In this lecture, we use Bandit, an open-source tool that parses Python code into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) to identify security bugs. We will write a script containing three critical vulnerabilities: 1. Hardcoded Secret (CWE-259) 2. SQL Injection Vector (CWE-89) 3. Command Injection Vector (CWE-78) 1

Code scanned: Total lines of code: 19 Total issues by severity: Medium: 0 High: 0 2.2 Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) 2.2.1 Theory and Core Concepts While SAST checks the text layout of our app, DAST requires a live, actively executing target network environment. DAST tools interact exclusively over application layers (HTTP/APIs), passing intentional attack payloads directly into active processing pipelines to observe structural runtime responses. Network Note for Students: Running an API inside Google Colab hosts the service on 127.0.0.1 (localhost) inside Google's cloud machine. You cannot open 127.0.0.1:8000 directly on your personal computer because your browser is looking at your own laptop, not the cloud machine. To allow external browser testing, we launch Localtunnel in the background so it doesn't freeze the environment, generating a secure public proxy URL. Localtunnel Security Landing Page: When you click the generated URL, you will see a security splash warning page designed to prevent anti-abuse. To unlock it: 1. Copy the Endpoint IP printed directly inside your Colab output dashboard. 2. Paste it into the "IP Address" box on the web page and hit submit. 3. p: LECTURE 3 Virtualization Security This lecture introduces the security of virtualized environments. It begins with the traditional server architecture that motivated virtualization, and then explains virtual machines, hypervisors, and the main benefits that virtualization provides. It next considers how cloud virtualization is secured, giving particular attention to hardware-based confidential computing through AMD SEV and Intel SGX and to the limitations of memory encryption. The lecture closes with four major virtualization threats: virtual machine escape, side-channel attacks, server-side request forgery, and insecure configuration. IN THIS LECTURE 3.1 3.2 3.3 3.4 3.5 3.6 Traditional Server Architecture Without Virtualization Virtualization and the Hypervisor Benefits of Virtualization Cloud Virtualization Security Confidential Computing in Cloud Virtualization Major Virtualization Threats 3.1 Traditional Server Architecture Without Virtualization In a traditional server environment without virtualization, an organization can have multiple physical servers, each dedicated to providing a different service to clients. Each physical server has its own hardware resources (CPU, RAM, and storage), an operating system installed directly on the hardware, and applications responsible for providing a particular service. For example, one physical server may host a website, another may manage email services, and a third may store and manage database information. Clients communicate with these servers over a network to request and receive the required services (Figure 3.1). Figure 3.1 A traditional server, with one operating system running on one set of hardware Although this approach provides dedicated resources for each service, it can lead to hardware underutilization, increased costs, higher power consumption, and additional maintenance, because each service requires separate physical hardware. These limitations 1

Lecture 3 | Cloud Virtualization Security motivated the development of virtualization, which allows multiple virtual servers to run on a single physical machine. 3.2 Virtualization and the Hypervisor 3.2.1 Virtual Machines Virtualization is a technology that allows multiple operating systems to run on a single physical machine by creating separate virtual computers called virtual machines (VMs). A virtual machine behaves like a physical computer: it has its own virtual CPU, memory (RAM), storage, operating system, and applications. However, instead of having dedicated physical hardware, each VM uses a portion of the resources allocated to it from the same physical machine. 3.2.2 The Hypervisor The hypervisor is a special software layer responsible for creating and running virtual machines, allocating physical CPU and RAM resources to each VM, and managing access to the physical hardware. PRACTICA L E X AMPLE Imagine a company has one powerful physical server. Instead of using three separate physical servers, it creates three virtual machines. VM 1 runs Linux and provides web services, VM 2 runs Linux and provides email services, and VM 3 runs Windows Server and manages databases. The hypervisor manages the physical resources and makes them available to these three VMs. There are two types of hypervisors, which differ in where they run relative to the physical hardware. 3.2.3 Type 1 Hypervisors A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the physical hardware without requiring a generalpurpose operating system underneath it. It controls the physical hardware resources and allocates them to the virtual machines running on it. When a physical server starts, the hardware becomes available, and the Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on it to create and manage multiple virtual machines, each of which runs its own operating system and applications (Figure 3.2). 2

Lecture 3 | Cloud Virtualization Security Figure 3.2 Four VMs running on a server with a Type 1 hypervisor 3.2.4 Type 2 Hypervisors Unlike Type 1, a Type 2 hypervisor runs as an application inside an existing operating system. The physical computer already has an operating system installed, and the hypervisor is then installed like an ordinary application. The operating system and the hypervisor work together to provide the resources needed by the virtual machines (Figure 3.3). This arrangement has four main layers. The physical hardware is the actual CPU, RAM, storage, and network devices. The host operating system is the operating system installed directly on the physical computer. The Type 2 hypervisor is a program installed on the host OS that creates and manages the VMs. Finally, the guest operating systems are the operating systems installed inside the virtual machines. Figure 3.3 A Type 2 hypervisor running as a program on a host OS, alongside other apps 3

Lecture 3 | Cloud Virtualization Security 3.3 Benefits of Virtualization Virtualization provides several important benefits that make managing computers and servers easier and more efficient. There are four fundamental benefits: partitioning, isolation, encapsulation, and hardware independence. 3.3.1 Partitioning Partitioning means dividing the resources of one physical computer among multiple virtual machines. The hypervisor allocates resources such as CPU, RAM, and storage to each VM, so that each VM operates as an independent computer even though all of them share the same physical machine. 3.3.2 Isolation Isolation means that each virtual machine operates separately from the other virtual machines. A problem inside one VM therefore does not normally affect the operation of the others. This is called fault isolation. Isolation also helps separate workloads and limit the impact of certain security incidents. However, it does not provide absolute protection against hypervisor vulnerabilities or attacks on shared hardware. 3.3.3 Encapsulation Encapsulation means that a virtual machine and its configuration can be stored as files. This makes it easier to copy, back up, move, and restore virtual machines. 3.3.4 Hardware Independence Hardware independence means that a virtual machine is not permanently tied to one specific physical computer. Because the VM uses virtual hardware provided by the hypervisor, it can often be moved to another compatible physical server without reinstalling its operating system and applications. 3.4 Cloud Virtualization Security Cloud virtualization is generally secure because cloud providers invest heavily in protecting their infrastructure. However, security is not guaranteed. Attackers may exploit weaknesses in virtualization software, CPU hardware, cloud applications, or security configurations. Three mechanisms contribute to the security of cloud virtualization. Hardware isolation means that each virtual machine operates in an isolated memory space, which prevents it from directly accessing another VM’s memory. Hypervisor security relies on the hypervisor to control the virtual machines and separate them from one another, while security patches fix weaknesses before attackers exploit them. Confidential computing uses technologies such as AMD SEV and Intel SGX to protect certain data during processing, reducing the risk of unauthorized access. 3.5 Confidential Computing in Cloud Virtualization Security This section focuses on two important hardware-based technologies: AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (AMD SEV) and Intel Software Guard Extensions (Intel SGX). Both help protect sensitive data while it is being processed, but they protect different things and use different keymanagement mechanisms. 4

Lecture 3 | Cloud Virtualization Security The central concepts are memory encryption, hardware-protected keys, and the security boundary. AMD SEV protects the memory of an entire virtual machine, whereas Intel SGX protects selected application code and data inside an enclave. 3.5.1 Introduction to Confidential Computing Cloud systems must protect data in three states. Data at rest is data stored on disks, databases, or other storage devices. Data in transit is data transferred between computers or services over a network. Data in use is data being processed by a CPU or another processing unit, usually while held in memory. Traditional encryption methods, such as disk encryption and TLS, protect data at rest and in transit. However, data often needs to be decrypted before a processor can use it. This creates a potential exposure if the host operating system, hypervisor, or another privileged component is compromised. Confidential computing addresses this problem by using hardware-based security mechanisms to protect sensitive data during processing. It establishes a protected execution environment in which selected data and code are isolated from software that is not trusted. In cloud virtualization, this is particularly important because multiple customers may share the same physical server. A cloud provider’s hypervisor manages the VMs, but customers may not want to rely entirely on the hypervisor to keep their data confidential. 3.5.2 Hardware-Based Memory Encryption Memory encryption protects data stored in physical memory (RAM) from unauthorized access by encrypting it before it is written to memory and decrypting it when it is read. 3.5.2.1 How Memory Encryption Works A simplified memory-encryption process consists of the following operations. 1. Data is processed by a VM. Applications and the guest operating system use data in the VM’s memory. 2. Encryption before storage. When data is written from the processor to physical memory, a hardware memory-encryption engine encrypts it. 3. Encrypted storage. The data is stored in RAM in encrypted form. 4. Decryption during access. When the processor reads the data, the memory-encryption engine decrypts it before making it available for processing. 5. Transparent operation. Encryption and decryption occur automatically in hardware, so applications generally do not need to perform these operations themselves. The objective is to prevent unauthorized software or physical memory inspection from reading sensitive information directly from RAM. 3.5.2.2 The AES Encryption Algorithm The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) is a widely used symmetric encryption algorithm, which means that the same secret key is used for encryption and decryption. AES supports three key sizes, with the number of rounds shown in Table 3.2. Table 3.2 AES key sizes and number of rounds AES key size Number of rounds AES-128 10 5

Lecture 3 | Cloud Virtualization Security AES key size Number of rounds AES-192 12 AES-256 14 AES processes data in fixed-size blocks of 128 bits. Its main encryption operations are SubBytes, which replaces each byte using a substitution table; ShiftRows, which shifts rows of the data block to rearrange the bytes; MixColumns, which combines bytes within each column to provide diffusion; and AddRoundKey, which combines the data block with a round key using an XOR operation. The final AES round does not include MixColumns. 3.5.2.3 What Is an Encryption Key? An encryption key is a secret value used by an encryption algorithm to transform readable data into encrypted data and to recover the original data. The memory-encryption engine, for example, uses a secret key to encrypt and decrypt memory contents. Without the correct key, an unauthorized party should not be able to recover the original plaintext from the encrypted memory contents, which is why the key must be protected: an attacker who obtains it may be able to decrypt the protected data. It is also important to distinguish between the encryption algorithm and the encryption key. AES is the algorithm; the secret key is the value used by AES. 3.5.3 Hardware-Based Key Generation and Management Memory encryption depends on secret keys, so protecting the encryption key is just as important as encrypting the memory itself. In confidential computing, keys are managed by hardware security components rather than being freely accessible to the operating system or hypervisor. 3.5.3.1 How Are Encryption Keys Generated and Protected? A hardware security mechanism typically performs the following functions. 1. Key generation. Creates a cryptographically secure secret key. 2. Key assignment. Associates the key with a particular VM or protected execution environment. 3. Key protection. Keeps the key inside a protected hardware boundary. 4. Key use. Allows the relevant hardware encryption mechanism to use the key without exposing it to untrusted software. 5. Key isolation. Prevents one VM or protected environment from using another environment’s key. Three related terms should be distinguished, as Table 3.3 shows. The exact mechanism differs between AMD SEV and Intel SGX. Table 3.3 Key generation, key derivation, and key management Term Meaning Key generation Creating a new secret key. Key derivation Producing a specific key from a protected root key and other inputs, such as an enclave identity. Key management Controlling the key’s assignment, use, protection, lifetime, and access. 3.5.4 AMD SEV: Protecting the Memory of an Entire Virtual Machine AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (AMD SEV) is a hardware-based security technology designed to protect the memory of a virtual machine from unauthorized access by the hypervisor 6

Lecture 3 | Cloud Virtualization Security or other software running outside that VM. Unlike application-level protection, AMD SEV aims to protect the memory of the entire guest VM. 3.5.4.1 Main Components of AMD SEV The AMD SEV architecture involves four important components. The guest virtual machine contains its own applications, guest operating system, and memory, and under AMD SEV its memory is encrypted when stored in physical memory. The hypervisor creates and manages VMs, allocating resources and controlling VM execution, but it is not supposed to have access to the plaintext contents of an SEV-protected VM’s memory. The AMD Secure Processor (AMD-SP) is a dedicated security component that performs security-related functions for SEV. It initializes and manages SEV security functions, generates or manages VM-specific memory-encryption keys, associates protected VMs with their encryption contexts, and keeps sensitive key material within a protected hardware environment. The hypervisor can request certain operations through the supported secure interface, but it cannot directly read the protected VM encryption key. Finally, the memory encryption engine is implemented in the processor’s memory-access path and automatically encrypts and decrypts VM memory as data moves between the processor and physical memory. 3.5.4.2 How AMD SEV Memory Encryption Works The process can be explained in the following steps. 1. Initialize the security mechanism. The AMD Secure Processor initializes the SEV functionality and its firmware. 2. Create a protected VM. The hypervisor creates a VM and requests that it be protected using SEV. 3. Associate an encryption key. A VM-specific memory-encryption key is generated or assigned through the hardware security mechanism. 4. Protect the key. The key remains protected and is not exposed to the hypervisor as plaintext. 5. Encrypt VM memory. When the VM writes data to physical RAM, the memory-encryption engine encrypts the data using the VM’s associated key. 6. Decrypt VM memory. When the VM reads its data, the processor decrypts it automatically before providing it to the VM. 7. Restrict unauthorized access. If the hypervisor attempts to inspect the encrypted VM memory directly, it cannot obtain the original plaintext data. 3.5.4.3 The VM Encryption Key (VEK) The Virtual Machine Encryption Key (VEK) is the secret key associated with an SEV-protected VM. It is used by the hardware memory-encryption mechanism to protect that VM’s memory. The processor uses the appropriate key when accessing each VM’s memory, which helps prevent the hypervisor or another VM from reading the protected memory contents. 7

Lecture 3 | Cloud Virtualization Security IMPOR TA NT D ISTINC TION ASID is not an encryption key. An Address Space Identifier (ASID) is an identifier used by the processor to distinguish address-space or encryption contexts. In SEV, it helps associate memory accesses with the appropriate VM encryption context. It does not encrypt data and is not a secret encryption key. 3.5.4.4 AMD SEV Security Extensions AMD SEV has evolved through several extensions, summarized in Table 3.4. Table 3.4 AMD SEV extensions and their main protection Technology Main protection SEV Encrypts VM memory to protect its confidentiality from the hypervisor. SEV-ES Adds protection for sensitive CPU register state when a VM exits to the hypervisor. SEV-SNP Adds memory integrity-related protections, including protection against certain malicious memory remapping and replay attacks. SEV-SNP is important because basic memory encryption primarily protects confidentiality. Encryption alone does not necessarily prevent an attacker from modifying encrypted memory or replaying previously observed memory contents. SEV-SNP adds protections intended to help detect or prevent certain forms of malicious memory manipulation, and it therefore strengthens the security of confidential VMs beyond basic memory confidentiality. 3.5.5 Intel SGX: Protecting Selected Application Code and Data Intel Software Guard Extensions (Intel SGX) is a hardware-based technology that protects selected application code and data inside a protected execution environment called an enclave. Unlike AMD SEV, which protects the memory of an entire VM, Intel SGX protects only the application components placed inside an enclave. 3.5.5.1 Main Components of Intel SGX Intel SGX involves four main components. The application outside the enclave is the ordinary application code that runs outside the protected environment; it may communicate with the enclave but is not automatically trusted. The enclave is a protected memory region containing selected application code and sensitive data. An application may, for example, place its cryptographic operations and secret keys inside an enclave while keeping other application functions outside it. The Enclave Page Cache (EPC) is a protected memory region used to hold enclave pages, and hardware security mechanisms protect the enclave’s contents against unauthorized access by the operating system or hypervisor. The CPU and SGX key hierarchy consists of hardwareprotected key material in the processor that is used to derive keys for SGX security operations. These keys are not directly exposed to the operating system or hypervisor. 3.5.5.2 How Intel SGX Protects Data The process works as follows. 1. Create an enclave. The application creates a protected memory region called an enclave. 2. Load protected code and data. Selected application code and sensitive information are placed inside the enclave. 8

Lecture 3 | Cloud Virtualization Security 3. Establish enclave identity. The processor establishes information about the enclave’s identity and security attributes. 4. Execute protected code. The application enters the enclave using an ECALL (Enclave Call). 5. Process sensitive information. The enclave performs sensitive operations, such as cryptographic calculations, using protected data. 6. Return results. The enclave exits through an EEXIT operation and returns permitted results to the application. 7. Protect enclave contents. The hardware prevents ordinary software, including the operating system and hypervisor, from directly reading the enclave’s protected memory. 3.5.5.3 How Are Keys Generated and Used in Intel SGX? Intel SGX uses a hardware-protected key hierarchy. Rather than allowing the operating system or application to create and freely access all enclave security keys, the processor derives keys from hardware-protected secret material. One important instruction is EGETKEY, which an enclave uses to request a key derived by the processor. The derived key depends on the requested key type and relevant enclave or platform security information. An enclave may, for example, request a sealing key to protect sensitive information that needs to be stored outside the enclave. The enclave then uses the derived key to encrypt or decrypt protected data, and the encrypted data can be stored outside the enclave. TH E IMPORTA NT P OINT The CPU derives the requested key. The operating system and hypervisor do not receive the underlying hardware-protected root secret. 3.5.5.4 Key Sealing Sealing is a mechanism that allows an enclave to encrypt sensitive data so that it can be stored outside the enclave and later recovered by an appropriately authorized enclave. The process involves five steps. 1. Generate or hold a key. An enclave generates or holds a sensitive cryptographic key. 2. Request a sealing key. The enclave requests a sealing key using EGETKEY. 3. Encrypt. The enclave encrypts the sensitive information using the derived sealing key. 4. Store. The encrypted information is stored outside the enclave, such as on a disk. 5. Recover. When the enclave needs the information again, it requests the appropriate sealing key and decrypts the stored data. 3.6 Major Virtualization Threats Cloud virtualization allows multiple virtual machines to share the physical resources of a single server. A hypervisor manages these VMs and provides isolation between them. This arrangement delivers flexibility, scalability, and efficient use of resources, but it also introduces security risks. An attacker may exploit vulnerabilities in the hypervisor, abuse shared hardware resources, attack cloud applications, or take advantage of insecure configurations. If these weaknesses are not addressed, the attacker may access sensitive information, compromise other VMs, or gain control over parts of the cloud infrastructure. This section examines three important threats, each of which targets a different part of the virtualization stack, as Figure 3.4 shows. Virtual machine escape attacks the isolation boundary enforced by the hypervisor. Side-channel attacks exploit the behavior of hardware that VMs 9

Lecture 3 | Cloud Virtualization Security share. Server-side request forgery (SSRF) abuses a vulnerable application to reach internal cloud services. Figure 3.4 The virtualization stack and the main threat that targets each layer 3.6.1 Virtual Machine Escape Definition Virtual machine escape is an attack in which an attacker compromises a VM and then exploits a vulnerability in the hypervisor or virtualization software to gain access to the host system or, in some cases, to other VMs. Normally, a VM operates in an isolated environment, and its operating system and applications should not be able to access the host operating system or another VM directly. VM escape occurs when an attacker bypasses this isolation. How the attack occurs Consider a cloud server running a hypervisor that hosts three VMs belonging to different customers. The attack unfolds in five steps, numbered in Figure 3.5 and in the list below. Figure 3.5 VM escape: from a compromised guest VM to the host system 1. Compromise a VM. An attacker exploits a vulnerability in an application or operating system running inside VM1. 2. Exploit virtualization software. After gaining control of VM1, the attacker sends specially crafted requests to a virtual device, such as a virtual network adapter or storage controller. 10

Lecture 3 | Cloud Virtualization Security 3. Trigger a hypervisor vulnerability. If the virtual device or hypervisor contains a security flaw, the malicious request may cause code to execute outside the VM’s isolated environment. 4. Escape the VM. The attacker gains unauthorized access to the host system or the hypervisor. 5. Attack other resources. Depending on the vulnerability and the attacker’s privileges, the attacker may access other VMs, interfere with their operations, or obtain sensitive information. 3.6.2 Side-Channel Attacks Definition A side-channel attack obtains sensitive information by observing indirect information about how a computer system operates, rather than by accessing the protected data directly. In cloud virtualization, multiple VMs may share physical CPU cores, cache memory, and other hardware resources. Although the hypervisor separates their virtual environments, some hardware activity can still reveal information through observable differences in execution time or resource behavior. How the attack occurs Consider two VMs belonging to different customers that run on the same physical processor (Figure 3.6). Figure 3.6 A cache side channel between two VMs on the same processor 1. Share physical hardware. The cloud provider runs VM1 and VM2 on the same physical CPU. 2. Execute sensitive operations. VM1 processes sensitive information, such as encryption keys or passwords. 3. Observe shared hardware behavior. The attacker controls a process inside VM2 and observes changes in shared CPU resources, such as cache activity. 4. Measure execution differences. The attacker measures how long certain operations take or observes cache access patterns. 5. Infer sensitive information. By analyzing repeated measurements, the attacker may infer information about VM1’s operations or potentially recover secret data. 11

Lecture 3 | Cloud Virtualization Security Side-channel techniques Cache attacks observe CPU cache access patterns and timing differences. Timing attacks measure execution time to infer information about sensitive operations. Speculative-execution attacks exploit CPU behavior to expose information through microarchitectural side effects. 3.6.3 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Definition Server-side request forgery (SSRF) is a web application vulnerability that allows an attacker to make a server send unauthorized requests to other systems or services. In cloud environments, an SSRF vulnerability may let an attacker reach internal services that are not directly accessible from the Internet, such as cloud management interfaces, internal APIs, or metadata services that provide information about the cloud instance. SSRF is primarily an application-layer vulnerability, but it becomes a serious cloud infrastructure threat when the vulnerable application has access to sensitive internal services. How the attack occurs Consider a cloud-hosted web application that lets users provide a URL so that the application can retrieve an image or download a file (Figure 3.7). Figure 3.7 SSRF: using a vulnerable server to reach internal cloud services 1. Identify a vulnerable application. An attacker discovers a web application that accepts a URL from users and retrieves content from it. 2. Provide a malicious URL. Instead of a normal public address, the attacker supplies a URL that points to an internal cloud service. 3. Cause the server to send a request. The application processes the URL and makes a request from the server’s own network environment. 4. Access an internal service. If the application can reach the requested service and the service does not adequately restrict access, the attacker may obtain information that should not be publicly accessible. 5. Abuse the obtained information. Depending on the service and the application’s permissions, the attacker may retrieve sensitive metadata or credentials and use them to access additional cloud resources. 12
