p: NETWORK SECURITY LABORATORY Experiment 2 – Configuring Switch Port Security Department: Cybersecurity Engineering Technologies | Fourth Year 1. Main Objectives      Understand the purpose of switch port security. Configure an access port and limit it to one MAC address. Use sticky MAC learning for the authorized computer. Detect and block an unauthorized computer. Recover a port disabled by a security violation. 2. Port Security in One Minute A switch normally learns MAC addresses automatically. Port Security restricts which MAC addresses are allowed to use an access port. In this lab, PC0 is authorized; when PC1 replaces it, the switch detects a different MAC address and shuts the port down. Key idea: Sticky learning automatically learns the first authorized MAC address and stores it as a secure MAC address. Term Meaning Access Port Connects an end device such as a PC. Secure MAC MAC address permitted on the protected port. Sticky MAC Automatically learned secure MAC address. Violation An unauthorized MAC attempts to use the secured port. 3. Violation Modes Mode Action Protect Drops unauthorized traffic. Restrict Drops traffic and records the violation. Shutdown Disables the port after a violation (used in this lab). Device IP Address Subnet Mask Role PC0 192.168.1.10 255.255.255.0 Authorized PC1 192.168.1.20 255.255.255.0 Unauthorized Network Security Laboratory – Experiment 2

4. Build and Configure the Network Add one Cisco 2960 switch and two PCs in Packet Tracer. Connect PC0 FastEthernet0 to Switch0 FastEthernet0/1 using Copper Straight-Through. Do not connect PC1 yet. Configure PC0 as 192.168.1.10/24 and PC1 as 192.168.1.20/24. Leave Default Gateway empty. 5. Initial Switch Setup enable configure terminal hostname S1 6. Configure Port Security on Fa0/1 interface fastEthernet 0/1 switchport mode access switchport port-security switchport port-security maximum 1 switchport port-security mac-address sticky switchport port-security violation shutdown no shutdown end Command Purpose switchport mode access Makes Fa0/1 an access port. port-security Enables port security. maximum 1 Allows one secure MAC address. mac-address sticky Learns the connected device MAC automatically. violation shutdown Disables the port when another MAC is detected. 7. Learn the Authorized MAC Generate traffic from PC0 so the switch can learn its MAC address: ping 192.168.1.20 The ping may fail because PC1 is not connected, but PC0 still sends traffic and the switch can learn its MAC address. Network Security Laboratory – Experiment 2

8. Verify the Authorized Device show port-security interface fastEthernet 0/1 show port-security address Expected Item Expected Value Port Security Enabled Port Status Secure-up Violation Mode Shutdown Maximum MAC Addresses 1 Sticky MAC Addresses 1 Violation Count 0 9. Test an Unauthorized Device Disconnect PC0 from Fa0/1. Connect PC1 to the same Fa0/1 port. From PC1, generate traffic using: ping 192.168.1.10 The switch sees a different MAC address. With shutdown mode, Fa0/1 is disabled. 10. Check the Violation show port-security interface fastEthernet 0/1 show interfaces status Item Expected Result Port Status Secure-shutdown Violation Count 1 Interface State May appear err-disabled Key idea: err-disabled means the switch automatically disabled the interface because of an error or security violation. 11. Recover the Port Disconnect PC1, reconnect PC0, then enter: enable configure terminal interface fastEthernet 0/1 shutdown no shutdown end show port-security interface fastEthernet 0/1 Expected state after recovery: Secure-up. 12. Save the Configuration copy running-config startup-config Network Security Laboratory – Experiment 2

13. Quick Troubleshooting Problem Check / Fix Port security command fails Configure switchport mode access first. Sticky MAC does not appear Generate traffic from PC0, then run show port-security address. Port remains red Reconnect PC0 and apply shutdown then no shutdown. PC1 is not blocked Verify Port Security: Enabled and Maximum MAC Addresses: 1. 14. Student Practical Task Create one switch and two PCs. Configure PC0 as the authorized device on Fa0/1. t: Cybersecurity Governance · L1 · Cybersecurity Governance: CIA, AAA & Controls
p: Middle Technical University LECTURE 1: CYBERSECURITY GOVERNANCE Foundations of Information Security, Protection Architecture & Enterprise Governance Course Module: CSTE4104 Topic: Governance, CIA/DAD, AAA & Controls Lecturer: Dr. Ammar Yahya Daeef Target Audience: 4 th stage Students Lecture roadmap      Security fundamentals and continuous improvement The five pillars of information security and the CIA Triad DAD, authenticity, nonrepudiation, and AAA services Protection mechanisms and security boundaries Security governance 1. Introduction Security helps an organization continue to exist and operate despite attempts to steal data or compromise its physical and logical assets. It is a business management responsibility, not merely an IT concern. IT/IS consists of the hardware and software that support business operations, while security protects their reliable and secure operation and supports the organization's mission, goals, and objectives. Organizations should adopt a security framework as a starting point and continuously evaluate and test their defenses. Three common evaluation methods are used: risk assessment, which identifies assets, threats, and vulnerabilities to determine risk; vulnerability assessment, which uses automated tools to find known weaknesses; and penetration testing, which uses trusted testers to stress-test defenses and discover issues before adversaries exploit them. Evaluation Methodology Risk Assessment Vulnerability Assessment Penetration Testing Primary Objective Identify assets, threats, and vulnerabilities to calculate overall exposure. Identify known software, hardware, and configuration weaknesses. Stress-test active defenses against simulated real-world adversarial attacks. Core Mechanism & Execution Evaluates impact vs. likelihood; establishes risk mitigation priorities. Employs automated scanning tools and baselining across networks and hosts. Conducted by ethical/trusted testers to find exploitable zero-days and logic gaps.

Organizations have limited budgets and must allocate resources wisely. Security controls should be selected to provide the greatest protection at the lowest reasonable cost, while meeting the organization's security needs. Security decisions should comply with applicable laws and be supported by appropriate evidence. This helps an organization defend its actions in court, respond to security breaches, and reduce the risk of fines, penalties, or negligence claims. Security is an ongoing process, not a project that can ever be considered complete. Technology, user behavior, vulnerabilities, and attack methods continually change. Therefore, organizations must regularly reassess their security infrastructure and improve their defenses because protections that were sufficient yesterday may not be sufficient tomorrow. 2. Understand and Apply Security Concepts The Five Pillars of Information Security: confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, and nonrepudiation. The first three form the CIA Triad, which represents the primary goals of information security. Security controls, vulnerabilities, and risks are evaluated according to how they affect these principles. 2.1 Confidentiality Confidentiality ensures that information is disclosed only to authorized individuals or systems. Unauthorized disclosure may result from deliberate attacks, human errors, poor security policies, or incorrectly configured controls. Common protections include encryption, access control, strong authentication, data classification, and employee training. Important related concepts include sensitivity (potential harm from disclosure),

discretion (controlling disclosure), concealment and secrecy (hiding or preventing disclosure), privacy (protecting personal information), seclusion (storing information in a restricted location), and isolation (keeping information separate). 2.2 Integrity Integrity protects the accuracy, correctness, and reliability of information by preventing unauthorized modifications and minimizing mistakes made by authorized users. It also ensures that data remains consistent and reflects reality. Threats include viruses, unauthorized access, software errors, malicious modifications, logic bombs, and backdoors. Common protections include access controls, strong authentication, intrusion detection, hash verification, input validation, and employee training. Key integrity concepts include accuracy, truthfulness, validity, accountability, responsibility, completeness, and comprehensiveness. 2.3 Availability Availability ensures that authorized users can access information and systems when needed, without unacceptable interruption. Threats include hardware failures, software errors, environmental problems, power loss, denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, and communication interruptions. Protection measures include performance monitoring, effective access controls, firewalls, redundant systems, reliable and tested backups, and fault tolerance. Business continuity planning (BCP) helps maintain critical services and eliminate single points of failure. Availability also involves three important concepts: usability (ease of use), accessibility (the ability of different users to interact with resources), and timeliness (providing access or responses within a reasonable time). QUICK MEMORY & RECALL MATRIX (THE CIA TRIAD) • Confidentiality: "Who can see or read the information?" (Restricting view) • Integrity: "Is the information accurate, valid, and unmodified?" (Preventing tampering) • Availability: "Can authorized users access systems and data on demand?" (Ensuring uptime) 2.4 DAD, Overprotection, Authenticity, Nonrepudiation, and AAA Services Beyond the CIA Triad, designing effective security policies and solutions requires evaluating additional principles such as the DAD Triad, the hazards of overprotection, authenticity, nonrepudiation, and comprehensive AAA services. The DAD Triad serves as the direct opposite and failure state of the CIA Triad, comprising disclosure (unauthorized access violating confidentiality), alteration (malicious or accidental changes violating integrity), and destruction/DoS (resources being damaged or made inaccessible, violating availability). Additionally, balancing security is critical because overprotecting confidentiality or

integrity can inadvertently restrict availability, whereas overproviding availability can destroy confidentiality and integrity. Other pillars include authenticity, which verifies that data is genuine and originates from its claimed origin, and nonrepudiation, which ensures that a subject cannot deny performing an action, supported through mechanisms like identification, authentication, authorization, auditing, accounting, digital certificates, and transaction logs. Finally, AAA services provide a foundational security mechanism spanning five operational elements that must be fully implemented to avoid structural vulnerabilities. The Five Elements of AAA Services AAA Element 1. Identification Operational Definition Claiming an identity. 2. Authentication Proving the claimed identity. 3. Authorization Granting specific permissions. 4. Auditing Programmatically recording activity. 5. Accounting (Accountability) Reviewing logs for compliance & holding subjects legally liable. Implementation Mechanism Usernames, smart cards, tokens, biometric identifiers. Passwords, PINs, OTP tokens, cryptographic certificates, biometric match. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC), ACLs. System event logs, access logs, intrusion logs (active logging vs passive monitoring). Log aggregation (SIEM), compliance reviews, forensic investigations, nonrepudiation.

3. Protection Mechanisms 3.1 Defense in Depth Protection mechanisms provide the structural integrity required to enforce security policies and safeguard systems against internal and external flaws. One of the most critical architectural strategies is defense in depth, which utilizes multiple layers of security controls to ensure that no single point of failure results in the exposure of systems or data.   Defense in Depth (Layering): o Defense in depth relies on implementing multiple security controls in a series rather than in parallel, ensuring that an attack is linearly evaluated and mitigated by every single security checkpoint. o While parallel configurations are useful in distributed computing, serial configurations are narrow and deep, meaning the failure of one control does not render the entire security solution ineffective. Related Architectural Terms: o  The text notes that terms such as levels, multilevel, layers, classifications, zones, realms, compartments, silos, segmentations, lattice structures, and protection rings are frequently used and should be understood within the context of defense in depth. Defense in Breadth (Diversity of Defense):

o Relying on security layers built from the same vendor or sharing common code is problematic because a single vulnerability can compromise multiple layers simultaneously. o Utilizing a range of security products from varied vendors significantly reduces or avoids the risk of a single exploit breaching several layers at once 3.2 Abstraction Abstraction serves as a vital operational principle designed to maximize efficiency by grouping similar elements into collective roles, classes, or groups that receive uniform security controls, permissions, and restrictions. Rooted in the principles of object-oriented programming (OOP), abstraction incorporates the unknown environment doctrine, which asserts that users or components do not need to understand the internal mechanics of an object, provided they know the correct syntax for sending inputs and receiving outputs. This doctrine mirrors mediated access models, where user-mode applications utilize system calls to request administrator-mode services, ensuring access requests are granted or denied based strictly on credentials rather than allowing unmediated access.   Simplification and Classification: Abstraction simplifies security administration by allowing administrators to classify objects or assign roles to subjects, streamlining the application of controls by type or function. Object Groups and Classes: Security administrators can define object groups or classes linked to job roles, making privilege management much easier because adding an object to a class automatically confers its assigned rights and privileges without separate individual management. 3.3 Data Hiding Data hiding serves as a critical security control and programming practice designed to prevent data from being discovered or accessed by placing it within a logical storage compartment that is completely invisible and unreachable to unauthorized subjects. Unlike security through obscurity, which merely relies on silence or secrecy and hopes an object remains undiscovered without implementing actual safeguards, data hiding provides real protection by isolating objects into separate security containers distinct from subjects who lack the authorization or means to access them.

   Definition and Examples: o Data hiding ensures that a subject cannot see or access data, rather than just keeping it temporarily unseen. o Practical implementations include protecting databases from unauthorized visitors, restricting lower-level classification subjects from accessing higher-level data, preventing applications from accessing hardware directly, and utilizing steganography. Role in Multilevel Secure Systems: o Data hiding is a vital characteristic in multilevel secure systems because it ensures that data existing at one security level is entirely invisible to processes running at different security levels. o From a security perspective, this relies on placing objects in security containers separate from those occupied by subjects who lack the need to know or the means to access them. Data Hiding vs. Security Through Obscurity: o Data hiding intentionally positions data so it is functionally unviewable and inaccessible to unauthorized subjects. o In contrast, security through obscurity is akin to digital hide and seek, where an organization hopes an object will not be discovered simply by keeping knowledge of it a secret without providing actual protection. o A classic example of security through obscurity occurs when a programmer releases software containing a known flaw, hoping that no one will discover the issue and exploit it. 4. Security Boundaries A security boundary serves as the critical line of intersection between distinct areas, subnets, or environments that maintain differing security requirements or needs. Recognizing these boundaries—such as the perimeter separating a local area network (LAN) from the public Internet—is essential for establishing reliable security barriers and deploying necessary mechanisms to control the flow of information. Furthermore, security boundaries can manifest as distinctions between object classifications, where specific rules define which subjects are authorized to perform functions on designated objects.   Physical vs. Logical Environments: o Security boundaries exist across both physical and logical domains, requiring distinct security mechanisms for each. o Both physical and logical security must be present for a complete structure and must be addressed separately within an organization's security policy. Perimeter Definition and Legal Responsibility: o Security policies must clearly define where control begins and ends in both environments. o Logical boundaries mark where electronic communications interface with organizationresponsible devices, whereas physical perimeters—such as office walls, building

 exteriors, or campus fences—frequently reflect the reach of the physical security policy and legal responsibility. Control Implementation and Cost Efficiency: o When translating security policies into actual controls, each environment and boundary must be evaluated separately to determine the most reasonable, cost-effective, and efficient solution. o All security countermeasures must be carefully weighed against the actual value of the protected objects, as deploying countermeasures that cost more than the protected assets is unwarranted. 5. Evaluate and Apply Security Governance Principles Security governance encompasses the collection of practices dedicated to supporting, evaluating, defining, and directing an organization's security efforts, optimally executed by a board of directors or a governance committee. In smaller organizations, these responsibilities may fall to the chief executive officer (CEO) or the chief information security officer (CISO). By comparing internal security processes with insights from external sources—often brought by diverse board members from various industries. Security governance aims to continuously improve organizational defense and resilience. Furthermore, security governance is closely intertwined with corporate and IT governance, sharing interrelated goals focused on maintaining business processes, driving growth, and minimizing downtime and potential loss.    Governance Drivers and Compliance: o Governance requirements are often imposed by legislative and regulatory compliance needs, industry guidelines, or licensing requirements. o All forms of governance must be assessed and verified periodically through auditing and validation, which can become complex when laws across different countries conflict. Security as a Business Operation: o Security must never be treated solely as a back-end IT issue; rather, it is a business operations issue and an organizational process that affects every aspect of the enterprise. o Using the term security governance emphasizes that security must be actively managed and governed throughout the entire organization, well beyond the boundaries of the IT department. Security Frameworks: o Organizations frequently adopt established security frameworks and governance guidelines—such as NIST SP 800-53 and NIST SP 800-100—to standardize and organize the otherwise complex process of implementing security governance.

o Although NIST guidance focuses heavily on government and military applications, it can be effectively adopted and adapted by commercial and private organizations as well. 6 Third-Party Governance Third-party governance establishes a system of external oversight mandated by laws, regulations, industry standards, contractual obligations, or licensing requirements, typically involving outside investigators or auditors designated by a governing body or hired as consultants. Beyond external audits, third-party governance also entails applying stringent security oversight to external entities that an organization relies upon, such as third-party providers handling security guards, maintenance, technical support, or accounting services. Because these outsourced partners must fully comply with the primary organization's security stance, failing to enforce this oversight introduces severe risks and vulnerabilities to the enterprise.   Compliance Verification and Auditing Protocols: o Third-party governance focuses heavily on verifying compliance with stated security objectives, regulations, requirements, and contractual obligations. o On-site assessments provide firsthand exposure to deployed security mechanisms. o Auditors conducting these reviews must follow established auditing protocols like Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies (COBIT) while utilizing a specific checklist of requirements. Open Document Exchange and Review: o The assessment process requires full and open document exchange between the target organization and the governing body so that all compliance requirements and concerns are mutually understood, thereby reducing unrealistic expectations. o Organizations must submit security policies and self-assessment reports back to the governing body. o Transmitting these files transitions naturally into a detailed documentation review process.

Alignment of Security Function to Business Strategy, Goals, Mission, and Objectives Security management planning ensures the proper creation, implementation, and enforcement of a security policy, aligning security functions with the strategy, goals, mission, and objectives of the organization. This includes designing and implementing security based on business cases, budget restrictions, or scarcity of resources. Business Case: A documented argument or stated position to define a need to make a decision or take some action, demonstrating a business-specific need to alter an existing process or choose an approach to a business task. It is often used to justify starting a new security-related project. Resource Limitations: Because money, people, technology, and space are limited in most organizations, the maximum benefit needs to be obtained from any endeavor. Top-Down Approach: One of the most effective ways to tackle security management planning. Upper or senior management initiates and defines policies for the organization to provide direction for all levels, while middle management fleshes out the security policy into standards, baselines, guidelines, and procedures. Bottom-Up Approach: The opposite of the top-down approach, where IT staff makes security decisions directly without input from senior management. This approach is rarely used and is considered problematic in the IT industry. Executive Roles in Strategy: The Chief Information Officer (CIO) focuses on ensuring information is used effectively to accomplish business objectives, while the Chief Technical Officer (CTO) focuses on ensuring equipment and software work properly to support business functions. 8. Organization Roles and Responsibilities Elements of security management planning include defining security roles, prescribing how security will be managed, assigning responsibility, and establishing testing methods. The best security plan is useless without senior management approval and commitment. Responsible for independently verifying and evaluating security controls, policies, and practices to ensure compliance with internal guidelines, regulations, and industry standards. 9. Due Diligence and Due Care Due Diligence: The research, investigation, and planning phase that involves discovering risks, evaluating third parties, and ensuring proper preparation. Due Care: The execution phase and practical operational procedures taken to protect assets, implement security policies, and prevent negligence or legal liability. Developing and implementing a security policy serves as tangible evidence of senior management's due diligence and due care. 10. Security Policy, Standards, Procedures, and Guidelines Security Policy: The top tier of formalization defining the scope of security, assets requiring protection, security objectives, vision, and goals. Policies can be organizational, issue-specific (e.g., network service, department), or system-specific. Standards: Define compulsory requirements for the homogenous use of hardware, software, technology, and security controls. Baselines: Define the minimum level of security that every system throughout the organization must meet before entering production. Guidelines: Offer recommendations and operational advice on how standards and baselines are implemented. Procedures: Step-by-step instructions detailing how to execute security operations. 11. Threat Modeling Threat modeling is a proactive engineering process used during application and system design to anticipate adversary tactics and prioritize defenses. 11.1 Threat Identification Approaches Threat modeling generally approaches threat identification through three primary perspectives: Attacker-Focused (Adversary-centric): Identifies potential attackers and evaluates their motivations, goals, capabilities, and attack vectors to anticipate how they might compromise the system. Software-Focused (Software-centric / System-centric): Deconstructs the software design, architecture, and code logic to uncover flaws, trust boundary issues, and vulnerable routines. Asset-Focused (Asset-centric): Starts by inventorying critical organizational assets and evaluates all potential threats that could endanger those specific assets. Understand and Apply Risk Management Concepts Risk management is the detailed process of identifying factors that could damage or disclose assets, evaluating those factors against asset values and countermeasure costs, and implementing cost-effective solutions to mitigate or reduce risk to an acceptable level. 12.1 Key Terminology & Concepts Asset: Anything used in a business process or task. If an organization relies on a person, place, or thing (tangible or intangible), it is an asset. Asset Valuation ($AV$): The assigned value of an asset based on importance, actual cost, nonmonetary expenses, and productivity impact. Threat: Any potential occurrence that may cause an undesirable outcome for an organization or a specific asset. Threat Agent / Actor: Entities (attackers, malware, disgruntled employees) that intentionally exploit vulnerabilities. Threat Event: Accidental or intentional occurrences (fire, system failure, power outage) exploiting vulnerabilities. Threat Vector: The path or means by which a threat agent gains access to a target (email, Wi-Fi, USB drives). Vulnerability: Weakness in an asset or absence of a safeguard/countermeasure. Exposure: Being susceptible to asset loss because of a threat. Lecture 1 Continuation - CSTE4104 Page 4 of 5

Risk: The possibility or likelihood that a threat will exploit a vulnerability to cause harm, expressed as: Risk = Threat × Vulnerability or Risk = Probability of Harm × Severity of Harm Safeguard (Countermeasure): Anything that removes or reduces a vulnerability or protects against threats. Reconfiguring existing elements or removing risky services are also valid safeguards. Attack: Intentionally exploiting a vulnerability by a threat agent. A malicious event does not have to succeed to be considered an attack. Breach: A successful attack where a security mechanism is bypassed or thwarted. Hazard: A potential source or situation that has the capability to cause harm or adverse consequences. 12.2 Cyclical Relationships of Risk Elements Threats exploit vulnerabilities, which results in exposure. Exposure is a risk, and risk is mitigated by safeguards.
